(jlace Bay, N.S., June 11.-After a pitched battle lasting upwards of fifteen minutes, striking United M.ne Workers of America miners recaptured the New U aterford power house station, shortly after noon to-day, and early this afternoon were in complete charge of the plant. Hon. G. H. Ferguson's announcement that the Dominion government was not disposed to give approval for the Nipissing Central railway extension into Rouyn came as somewhat of a surprise after the supposedly well-informed buying of Noranda shares on Thursday had carried that stock up to a new high record price.
Has the minister any further information on this subject?
Hon. GEORGE P. GRAHAM (Minister of Railways):	Mr. Speaker, the situation, I
think, has been fairly well stated before. The Nipissing Central Railway Company, owned by the Ontario government, asks the federal government to pass an order in council giving them the right to proceed upon crown lands belonging to the province of Quebec, through which they may build a railway. The province of Quebec takes very strong exception to the right of the federal government to pass any such order in council. The government has decided to refer the matter to the Supreme court to decide what are the rights of the respective parties.
Has the government not frequently, and indeed as a matter of course, passed those orders at other times?

Not under similar circumstances. I am told that on one occasion they did pass an order in council allowing the Canadian Pacific to enter upon crown lands. But the province of Quebec takes the stand very strongly that the cases are not similar.
What is the difference?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
There was no opposition in the
first case. Also, it was many years ago. I associate myself with what my colleague the Minister of Railways has said. The two provinces are taking absolutely opposite position? in the matter. The law authorities of the province of Quebec claim that this government has no right to confer authority on the railway company to take possession of provincial crown lands. On the other hand, the law officers of the province of Ontario claim that not only has this government power to do so, but it has no discretion in the matter, it has no right to withhold consent. In view of these two important provinces taking such different attitudes on a question of law, I

maintopic: INCOME WAR TAX ACT, 1917. REPEAL OF SECTION 25 CONSTITUTING LIEN UPON ASSETS OF TAX PAYER
speechtext:
Before this bill is read a third time, I think I should make a statement. When the bill was up for its

Bankruptcy Act
second reading, I suggested that in view of the fact that the committee on Public Accounts might have under consideration certain other amendments to the Income War Tax Act, it might be advisable to leave the bill over until those other possible amendments could be incorporated with the present bill. Since then I have had some conversation with the Acting Minister of Finance, and I understand that he is quite willing that any recommendations coming from the committee, when it is empowered to consider the matter, will be given sympathetic consideration by the government.
I have already given notice of a motion to authorize the committee to consider amendments to the act, but I should like before the third reading of this bill is gone on with to have some assurance from the minister that the motion of which I have given notice will not be opposed by the government, and that the government is prepared to consider sympathetically any suggestions that may come from the committee. I have no opposition to the present bill so far as it goes, and my only reason for asking for delay is that there may be other amendments which we might wish to incorporate in this bill. I would like to have a statement from the Acting Minister of Finance on that.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
This is to prevent a
conflict which has happened on some occasions. When an authorized assignment is made, the official receiver appoints a custodian. Now, nothing prevents a creditor from presenting a petition afterwards to declare the debtor bankrupt, and then under section 5 of the act an interim receiver may be appointed. A contest then develops between the interim receiver and the custodian. Their du ies are the same, and there is no necessity or even justification, for appointing an interim receiver when a custodian has been already appointed by the official receiver. This is suggested by Mr. Justice Panneton, a judge in bankruptcy in Montreal, and many others.

I entirely agree with what my hon. friend says. It is the height of ridiculousness to- have two officials, and to have duplication and two sets of costs. Suppose the section -were to read thus?-
The court may, if it be shown to be necessary for the protection of the estate. . . . appoint an interim receiver.
Bankruptcy Act

As my hen. friend poin'.s out we are now saying that this is not to be done if there is a custodian there already If (here is a custodian there it never could be shown to be necessary This provision seems to me to be flying in the face of common sense. It does seem to me that the House is called upon to say there are some judges so stupid that notwith-s anding the fact there is already a court officer appointed for the purpose of looking after the estate they may appoint another one although they have no jurisdiction to make any appointment whatever except in case of necessity. If my hon. friend, as Minister of Justice and the shepherd of the administration of justice in this country, says that such a thing is necessary for our courts why there is an end to it, but it seems to be ridiculous.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
It appears that if not
necessary it is expedient to have it.
Well, I am sorry to know that there is necessity for such expedient.

On section 4-Administration of insolvent farmers' estates by provincial government officer.

Before the section carries
I should like to ask the minister if he would not make some change in subsection (3) of this section which reads:
In case any such provincial officer is appointed custodian and trustee, he shall not be entitled under thi3 act to be paid any remuneration as custodian or trustee nor any of the costs enumerated as costs of custodian in part 3 of the general rules.
As I understand the subsection the provincial officer who becomes trustee under this net will not be allowed to collect any fees whatever for the work he may have in connection with the administration of that estate. It seems to me that would be putting quite a burden upon the provincial government. We -all know that -the provincial governments in western Canada are hard up. I think however, they would not object to paying a custodian's expenses in such cases, for instance, as those where the estates were not sufficient to cover these costs; but surely they should be entitled to a fee which would cover their office expenses in connection with these estates Which they do administer. I do not think there would be any desire on the part of the provincial government to make any money out of this scheme; but I think there should be provision made here to entitle them to such fees as were necessary 
to pay for the expenses they must incur in the administration of these estates. I should like to ask tihe minister if he would not make some amendment which would permit that.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The justification for this amendment is that it is intended to reach a special case where the farmers referred to in the section have not sufficient property to warrant the administration of their estate in the usual way. The argument advanced was -that it would not cost anything and that the provincial officer would be paid by the province. The section has been accepted with that understanding. It is exactly what was recommended by the committee on Banking and Commerce last year. It is also what was suggested by the Canadian Council of Agriculture, and, I think, by my hon. friend himself last year.

I have been in consultation
with the Attorney General for the province of Allberta regarding this act, and I think he is very pleased with the amendments that are being brought down, with -the exception of this one. The reason that many farmers could not take advantage of the Bankruptcy Act was, that when they went to the trustee they were required by him -to place in his hands, as a deposit to guarantee his expenses, possibly $100 and in some cases $150. This amendment would obviate that difficulty. The provincial officer who acts as trustee under the act would now receive that man's application (for bankruptcy without requiring any deposit; but after he has administered the man's affairs, and in some cases incurred considerable office expenses, why should the provincial government be required to pay the whole of that and not collect any fees? That is the only change I should like to see in this section.

Bankruptcy Act

In this particular case I am, for at least once, in hearty accord with the minister. I find myself thoroughly in agreement with the minister in this case. In Saskatchewan we have an adjustment bureau which is already handling many cases of this kind, and I think the authorities have already intimated that they would handle these cases without cost. I see no particular trouble in Saskatchewan.

My understanding is
along this line: That the chief difficulty today in the way of the farmers being able to take advantage of the provisions of the Bankruptcy Act is caused by the fact that their assets must represent fifty per cent of their liabilities; and if their assets do not represent fifty per cent of the liabilities they will not, under the law as it stands to-day, be granted a clearance by the court. Is that right?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The judge has a certain discretion in the matter. Ordinarily the farmer would have to wait two years to get his discharge, if his assets were not fifty per cent of his liabilities, but the judge might shorten that period.
Is it not the fact that the assets must represent at least fifty per cent of the liabilities before he will be granted a discharge?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: He cannot be granted a discharge immediately unless the assets are fifty per cent of the liabilities; the law provides that he will have to wait two years for his discharge, but if that is the only reason why the discharge cannot be granted immediately, the judge has a discretion in the matter, and may shorten the time.
At the expiration of two years may the judge grant the discharge?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes.

I am glad to hear the minister say that, but there are not many farmers in western Canada whose assets
would amount to fifty per cent of their liabilities. For that reason, if the provisions of the law were to remain as they are, they would not be of very much use to the farmer who desired to take advantage of it.

I cannot oppose this measure, but I think the minister is wrong in contending that the provincial government should bear the expense of putting all these farmers through bankruptcy. I argued this case with my hon. friend's predecessor in office some time ago, when I wished him to appoint an official receiver who would receive assignments from the bankrupt farmer who could not afford to put up the deposit required, and the then Minister of Justice (Sir Lomer Gouin) said:
I cannot agree with you that it is a right principle that the government should pay for putting people through bankruptcy.
That is what he is compelling the provincial. government to do through this act. If the man has some estate, and goes to this officer and has him act as his trustee in bankruptcy, why should that officer not be entitled to some fee to cover the out-of-pocket expenses in administering the estate of this man? In some cases there is considerable expense and under the act the provincial government has to pay all the 4 p.m. expenses which may be incurred in connection with the case. I think that the man's estate, if it is worth anything, should pay the expenses, and I cannot see that there is any need to place it all on the provincial government. I am sure the provincial government will accept it, if that is the best they can get, to help out the bankrupt farmer, but it is putting an unfair burden on the government.

maintopic: FRUIT ACT AMENDMENT BILL SENATE AMENDMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am opposed to this amendment entirely. My main reason is that there is no such body as the Horticultural Council of Canada, and I suggest that it is not reasonable to insert a wrong description. There is a body whose name is the Canadian Horticultural Council. I am further opposed to the amendment because it cuts right across the main object of the section, which was to facilitate the creation of grades which are not included in the Fruit Act. To refer this matter to a body such as the Canadian Horticultural Council may result in wery considerable delay, as that council is composed of the representatives of the fruit and vegetable interests all over Canada and it is only at the annual meeting that matters such as this are considered. This very matter has been discussed at considerable length in the conventions of the fruit growers' associations in
different parts of the Dominion; it has also been discussed at the annual meeting of the Canadian Horticultural Council. Matters such as this are frequently discussed between the fruit interests of America and of Canada. The fruit growers are perfectly satisfied with the clause as originally drawn, and I do not think it would be in their interests that the Horticultural Council of Canada should be brought into consultation, even if the name was correct. But my main reason for opposing the amendment is that it would be inserting in the bill reference to a body which does not exist.

Yes, we have a very complete method of control. From the evidence reported in the press as having been given yesterday before the Public Accounts committee by the Auditor General, there might be an impression that there is not a complete audit in the system, but there is a very thorough audit within the Finance Department. In order that hon. members may have it before them, I think I had better put on record a complete statement of the methods employed
in this connection. The statement is as follows:
Treasury board minutes passed in 1881 and 1910, authorized a certain procedure in connection with the management of Dominion currency and the audit thereof by the Auditor General. Naturally the growth of business in the interval has rendered obsolete many of the provisions of these orders, and as a consequence, a revised departmental procedure and system of verification and check as between the various branches at Ottawa and the offices of the Assistant Receivers General throughout the country came into effect. A complete control is maintained and an internal audit is made by an experienced staff.
I may say here that we audit up every night before the staff leaves. If hon. gentlemen would care to go through the department and observe personally the system that is followed, I should be glad to have someone take them through-though not all at once; we would not like to take more than four or five at a time. The members of the staff are all locked inside there and no one is allowed to leave until a complete balance is made at the end of the day. The statement continues:
The present system was approved of by Messrs. Edwards Morgan and Company, chartered accountants of Toronto, in connection with the audit and supervision of departmental practice which they conducted in 1921 and 1922.
The Treasury board in January 1925, passed a minute, copy attached, outlining in detail the procedure at present followed by the Department of Finance. The following is quoted therefrom:-
"The board are of the opinion that the procedure outlined above is well designed for the protection of the currency and direct that the said procedure be recognized as the one to be followed in the management of the Dominion Currency.
"It appears to the board that down to the point where worn or mutilated notes are received by the department to be destroyed, no further check is required than that provided for as above described, but that before the said worn or mutilated notes are destroyed they should be examined by the Auditor General as prescribed by section 17 of the Consolidated Revenue and Audit Act."
The Auditor General has not made an audit of the note reserves held at Ottawa since some years prior to the commencement of the war, nor has he made any requests to do so. From 1910 to 1913, the Auditor General's department sent officials to our outside offices, at which stores of notes and gold are kept. Men inexperienced in handling securities, unfamiliar with vault combinations, and incapable of assuming the full control necessary to make an effective audit were sent on these inspection trips. The inspection was valueless, and the result was to create a bad impression on the stafl of our offices. During the war the audit of outside offices by the Auditor General was discontinued, and no requests had since been made by him for facilities from the Department of Finance in that connection. It is apparent, therefore, that the only audit of currency which the Auditor General has been conducting is that of redeemed notes for destruction, as called for by the Audit Act. This audit has been a casual one-
I would ask the hon. gentleman to observe this:

The intention was that the Board of Audit should go very carefully into the affairs of the different departments, devise a system to prevent overlapping in each department, and effect economies. I was not in

I have not that before me yet but I will get my right hon. friend a statement.

For this evening?

Supply-Finance
I should like to get these votes cleaned up before six o'clock and go on with another department.

Before eight o'clock
then?
I do not think I can; I will give it to my right hon. friend to-morrow.
Will the minister have some estimates under which we can discuss this matter?
Of the Finance department? I am not sure, but if not we can discuss it in connection withj any * other department that I am interested in.

Item agreed to.
Expenses in connection with the negotiation of treaties, $20,000.
Is this to pay the expenses of the minister?

This item, to provide for expenses in connection with the negotiation of treaties, was first included in the estimates for 1922-23, and at that time with the cattle embargo conference. The expenditure in 1922-23 was $8,264.83. In 1923-24 there was no expenditure. Up to February 20, 1925, the expenditure was $2,579.06.

What about all those
trips round the world in the negotiation of treaties? They cannot be included.
My right hon. friend will find a return of my expenses in the Auditor General's department, I believe they will compare very favourably with his own travelling expenses when he was Prime Minister.

They will not be any
less.
Do not be too sure about that.
I guarantee it right now. However, I was not speaking of the amount of the expenses, I was saying that they cannot be included in this item.
They are not in this item.
What has this to do with the negotiation of treaties, which has been largely a matter of voyaging?

My right hon. friend will
observe that in 1923-24 there was no expenditure. In 1922-23 there was an expenditure of $8,264.83. I have not the details but my right hon. friend will remember that the Minister of Finance in that year negotiated a
treaty with France and, I think, with Italy, but I am not sure whether the expenses on that occasion are included in the amount or not. As to the expenditure up to February 20, 1925, of $2,579.06, I do not know what it represents.

I should like to know
first what portion of the expenses this covers. It does not cover the entertainment of the treaty makers; that is in the one before. What could it cover?

This does not include all but
I am told some of this expense was incurred by the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) in going down to Washington. I am not very sure-I should not like to be quoted as saying it-whether part of the expenses of the gentleman who went to the West Indies is charged here, but I will get full details for my right hon. friend.
That is what I would like to know-what this covers; and what jaunts are in mind this year.

I will get that information
for my right hon. friend.

Mr. Ross is still at sea is
he?
Yes, I am told he is likely to land at Sydney on the thirteenth. If he goes by rail, he will be in Melbourne before the sixteenth.

Is that the reason why
the government are trying to hurry the session -so that there will be no chance of getting the Australian treaty through?

I will be glad to hear that
there is any prospect of getting it through.
Will the minister say the trip of Mr. Ross is included under this item?

I would not think so. He is
an officer of the department and his expenses are charged up to the department.

So are the expenses of
the Minister of Justice. For the life of me I do not know what can be included in this item. It is a new item, it was put in by this government.

Yes. It was first included in
the estimates for 1922-23.

Has the minister had
representations from numerous firms in Canada urging that the Australian treaty should be ratified?

Yes.
Supply-Finance

I have had a number
of letters myself from men in New Brunswick who had quite a large trade with Australia and they say that, due to the suspension of this treaty or the uncertainty about it, no one in that dominion will do business with them. They are waiting to know what the terms of the treaty will be, expecting there is a possibility of better terms.
That is good news.

Well, it might be
better. At the present time they say the business they did have is entirely suspended; that no one will order goods from Canada because they are waiting to get the benefit of this treaty. I think it is urgent that the matter be hastened as much as possible.
I agree with my hon. friend.

I should not like to
accept the idea the leader of the opposition has advanced that this session would be over before anything would be done about it. If that is likely, is it possible for the government to negotiate this treaty during the recess? Or must it be ratified by parliament?
I would not commit myself as to that.
Because if not, parliament might give the government whatever authority is necessary to negotiate this treaty.

I have nothing to add to the
statement made by the Prime Minister. I do not think it is wise to state anything further.

I should like to get information as to the authority of the government to negotiate a treaty when the House is not in session. I think we passed an act two years ago authorizing the government to negotiate a reciprocity agreement with the United States if the opportunity ever offered. I should like to urge the government very strongly, if this Australian treaty is not consummated and ready for ratification before the House prorogues, to bring down a bill and obtain authority to ratify this treaty, such treaty to be submitted to parliament at its next session for confirmation if necessary; at any rate, that the government should have authority to deal with this treaty when the negotiations have been completed by its representative who is now in Australia.
Why does the hon. member want an assurance that the government will pass and sign the treaty when he does not know what is in it?

I presume that our
government would not negotiate a treaty that would be to the disadvantage of Canada. The representations I have from business men in New Brunswick, amongst them the canners of fish are that the terms as proposed would give Canadian business great advantages in Australia.
I cannot find what they are.

I have not been able to either. I do not know what these people have in mind. In their letters to me they indicate they did have an idea that it would be of great value to their in'.erests. If there is anything we can do to assist business in Canada by a treaty or otherwise, it is our duty to do it.
I have not as great faith as the apostle of Israel to my left-

My hon. friend is almost
alone in Canada in that respect.	[DOT]

I almost have a feeling
I would like to be alone when I see the hon. member approadhing. The speech of the hon. member to my left (Mr. Caldwell) exemplifies about what everybody in Canada knows about this treaty. Business men seem to be able to make a guess. They are permit' ed by the government to make a guess with impunity. Australia is permitted to publish what it believes to be the treaty. The United States representatives are permitted to send to- their government what they believe to be the treaty. In fact everybody is permitted to do what he likes and to know what he likes about the treaty except the parliament of Canada; but the constitution would -crash if this government gave the least intimation to hon. members of the House as to what is in the treaty. Not only have we not the right to know what is in ;he treaty that this government is about either to execute or abandon but we are not permitted to know what the object of the present mission of Mr. Ross is. We are told, or it is intimated to us at least, that the government is not satisfied with some clause about Australia requiring goods that get the preference from us to be 75 per cent manufactured in Canada. This is as far as anybody will go in the way of letting parliament know what is the reason for the delay or what is the object of the Ross mission. But anyone who reviews the terms of the treaty and the facts of the actual trade of Canada knows that that clause has mighty little significance,-I do not say it has none but

Supply-Finance
it has very little, for the simple reason that the goods we sell are made more than 75 per cent in our own country. Will the minister say now whether there is any other objec' in Mr. Ross' visit, save to review this one clause and adjust it satisfactorily? Has there been some proposal given Mr. Ross to transmit to Australia, altering the alleged treaty in some other way? Are those terms thar are advertised by the plenipotentiaries of other countries as the terms of the treaty really the terms of it? If so, is there some particular besides the one the hon. gentleman has referred to that the government is not satisfied with? If there are any people in this world, I would think, who had the right to know what was in this treaty at this stage, i: is surely the representatives of the people of Canada. Are these one-time, sometime apostles of the rights of parliament, of the true underlying principles of democracy, these decriers of autocracy, these people who would; restore responsible government,-are these to be those who hide and continue to hide the essential elements of a really important treaty from the parliament of Canada long after the parliaments of other countries have been advised? Is the minister prepared to accept that as the situation and allow parliament to be dissolved and the treaty to be still at sea when we come home after the fourth session?

I do not think any good purpose can be served by discussing this matter. I am sure my right hon. Mend is as anxious as I am to have a favourable trade agreement with the sister dominion of Australia. I am satisfied of this, because men with whom he himself was closely associated, made an attempt on two different occasions to make such an agreement.
Just one.
Sir Mackenzie Bowell and Sir George Poster?
That was before my time.

I am frank to say this: That
there are those in Australia and there are those-well I would not say in Canada, but there are those on this continent-who are not anxious this trade agreement should be consummated.
In Canada, did the minister say?

I do not think any good
purpose can be served by a discussion of the matter, and I do not wish to be drawn into such a discussion.

I received a letter from a certain business man in New Brunswick about a month ago. He said that in conversation with a member of the manufacturers' association, that gentleman said to him that the reason this treaty was not ratified was on account of the opposition of the Progressives in this parliament. In reply to him I said there had been no opposition by anybody, because no treaty had been submitted to the House, and it was pretty hard to say whether we would support it or not until we heard what it was. I wonder just how the member of the manufacturers' association got that impression. The minister said he would hesitate about saying that there were people in Canada who might be opposed to the treaty; and so far as I am personally concerned I wish to disclaim any opposition to the treaty until I know what is in it, and I do not wish to be under the imputation that I am against it, as has been suggested by the member of the manufacturers' association.

I am sorry if I have created
the inference that it was representative of the people in the House of Commons that might be opposed to it; that was not what I had in mind at all. But there are certain strong interests, both in Australia and in the continent of America, that are doing the best they can to create divisions, and I do not think any good purpose can be served by a further discussion at this moment.

What portion of the
continent of America does the minister refer to?

I would rather not go any
further.
In Canada?
I am not going to discuss it.
Wrangel island?

After Recess

Before recess the leader of
the opposition (Mr. Meighen) asked for information with reference to certain exenditures between the years 1922 and 1925 in connection with this vote. The following expenditures were made in connection with the negotiation of treaties in 1922-23:

Trade Arrangement with Spain-

Mr. W. McL. Clarke	 2,015 31

Mr. Clarke is our trade agent at Milan, in Italy, and this expenditure was incurred in connection with a trade arrangement which we have been completing with Spain.

I understand that before
six o'clock we were discussing the Australian treaty. Can the minister tells us what progress has been made in that direction?
I cannot give any information in that regard at present.

What progress has the government made in the matter of treaty negotiations with the United States? I believe there is a standing offer from this government to the United States, made by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding).
The United States has not responded as favourably as we desired, but we are not without hope that a more favourable attitude will be assumed in Washington towards Canada.

How favourably have
they responded?

Well, not as far as we would
wish.
Will my hon. friend indicate just what they have done in the way of response ?

No, I could not.
.

I did not think he
could.

Have the government
renewed their activities in that regard?
When we appoint an envoy at Washington he will probably make things go a little more rapidly.

Would it not be wise
on the part of the Acting Minister of Finance or the government to make some gesture in order to satisfy hon. gentlemen to my left? They do not need to make any to satisfy themselves.

Is not the appointment of
an envoy a gesture?
Mostly so.

Item agreed to.
Grant to the National Battlefields Commission-
(a)	For expenses of administration	
$ 6,000(b)	For maintenance of the National Battlefields Park	
30,000(c)	For maintenance of Martello towers,numbers 2 and 4	
1,000(d)	For new works in the park	
142,000

What is being done by
the commission?

Are these moneys spent
entirely in the province of Quebec?

On the battlefield of Quebec
where Wolfe and Montcalm fought.

Is the vote limited to that
one particular battlefield1?
Yes, by act of parliament.

What are the
Martello towers, Nos. 2 and 4?

They must be somewhere
along the ramparts of Quebec. I am not sure whether they are near Wolfe's Cove or not.

It means that the
towers are part of the battlefield?
Yes.

Was all the appropriation
spent last year?
Yes.
I am thoroughly in sympathy with the purpose of the vote, but it seems to me a very large sum of money for that one particular place.

It is very much smaller than
it- used to be.

Item agreed to.
Grant in aid of the Canadian General Council of the Eoy Scouts Association, $15,000.

Will the minister give us
some details?

The Canadian General Council of the Boy Scouts Association aids in a general way the objects of the movement in Canada. The officers are: chief scout, Baron Byng of Vimy; chief commissioner, Dr. James W. Robertson; assistant chief commissioner, John A. Stiles; dominion secretary, Gerald Brown; hon. treasurer, D. M. Finnie From 1914-15 up to 1921-22 they were given 85,000 a year. Since 1922-23 they have received $15,000 a year.

Item agreed to.
Contribution to aid in carrying on the work of the Royal Astronomical Society, $2,000.
Why is this vote? We have our own two observatories.

This vote has been in the estimates since 1910-11. The society is for the purpose of stimulating and encouraging the study of astronomical subjects. The vote is for the publication of the journal and handbook and for public meetings. Revenue is derived from grants by the Dominion and provincial governments and by the city of Toronto and the University of Toronto. There is a further revenue from the fees of members.

Mr. Chairman, the other evening we had votes for the Dominion observatory at Ottawa and the Victoria observatory, and we were given to understand that a large percentage of the money was for the issue of publications. Is there not a possibility of duplication here, if both the observatories and this society are carrying on similiar work? As the right hon. leader of the opposition said, the United States with its large population has only two observatories.
This is a very small vote, and the society receives some assistance from the provincial governments as well as from the city of Toronto and the University of Toronto.
What provincial governments? Do all of them subscribe?
I could not tell my right hon. friend.

Does it say provincial
government or governments?
Provincial governments.
Has the minister any account of the accomplishments of the society?

No; there may be in the
library.

Mr. Chairman, with the little information at our disposal at the moment, I am not prepared to suggest the striking out of this vote, but in view of the amount of money which is already being spent by the government on astronomical work, I submit that we are scarcely justified as a committee in going much further without fuller information. What is the nature of the work being performed? And just why is this sum voted? Can any scientific society come to the administration and ask for two or three thousand dollars and get it without giving some reasons? If there are any reasons, what are they?

If we made grants to all the societies that applied to us the supply bill would be much larger than it is. I cannot give my hon. friend any further information.
Item agreed.
Grant to the Royal Society of Canada, $8,000.

In view of the amendments to the Criminal Code introduced the other evening by the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe), I presume it might be well to amend this vote by striking out the word "Royal."
Supply-Finance

The hon. member's information is a little scant. This society was organized with the full approval, both as to name and purpose, of Her Majesty the Queen at that time. I would strongly recommend to the member for Bow River that he attend some of its sessions and not only listen to the addresses, but read its literature. In that I am not intending to pay any compliment to myself.

Item agreed to.
Royal Canadian Academy of Arts, $2,500.
This is new to me.

It has been in the estimates
since 1910-11. The object is to promote interest in the fine arts. The members of the academy give their services gratuitously. Free classes are held at large centres throughout the Dominion. Grants are made to the Toronto and other large exhibitions. The president is G. Home Russell; vice president, Henry Sproatt; secretary, E. Dyonnett; treasurer, C. W. Simpson.
Does the minister know any of them?

No, I have not that pleasure. From 1910-11 to 1912-13 they received $2,000 a year, but in 1913-14 the government of the day increased their grant to $5,000 and this continued until 1916-17. In 1917-18 it was reduced to $2,500 and they were paid that amount until 1920-21. In 1921-22 they were given $7,500 and in 1924-25 the grant was reduced to $2,500.

Item agreed to.
Grant to the Inter-parliamentary Union for Peace. $400.

What are
the activities of this organization with respect to peace?

This amount has been voted
annually since 1914-15. The secretary is Mr. Charles Lange, with headquarters at Geneva. They have been paid $200 each year.

What is
the work they are doing?

They have annual meetings,
and so on.

Are they associated with the
League of Nations?
I could hot say.

Why is * the amount
doubled this year?

My recollection is that this
year they meet in Washington and I think it is expected that they will come to Canada.
The $200 is to entertain them here, is it?
No, I think there is another grant for that.

It seems rather ridiculous to be spending $400 on organization for peace When we are spending about $12,000,000 on preparations for war, or on so-called defence. If there was anything worth while in this organization I would be prepared to support a much larger grant. We ought to know something more about it.

Item agreed to.
Civil Government-Insurance-salaries, $80,350; contingencies, $61,000.
Mr. MAN'ION: Why the increase?

The increase is due to one promotion, senior actuary to chief actuary, A. D. Watson, $675; one promotion, senior actuarial examiner to chief examiner, W. H. Gilliland, $675; one promotion, statistical clerk to senior statistical clerk, H. A. Urquhart, $360; statutory increases, $2,130; one clerk additional, $960. That accounts for the increase.

This is the department where the minister strolls around and goes into nearly every business in the country. I see in the details that the salary of the Superintendent of Insurance is now raised to $10,000 a year.
It has been at that figure for some time. The cost of the administration of this office is paid by the insurance companies.

No it was made last year, I think, or the year before, because I remember receiving circulars opposing it. The increase may not have been from $5,000 to

Supply-Finance
$10,000; at any rate it was made $10,000 at that time. I have nothing to say against Mr. Finlayson in any shape or form, but this does seem a pretty heavy salary in view of the fact that most of our deputies receive $6,000 to $8,000.

My recollection is that the
increase was made at the request of the people who pay the expenses, the insurance companies themselves. Mr. Finlayson is a most excellent officer, and when you compare the salaries that are paid to managers of insurance companies with the salary that Mr. Finlayson receives, I think we have him at a very reasonable rate. Mr. Finlayson was not appointed by this government, but by my predecessor Sir Thomas White, and I recall that the last time I met Sir Thomas White he told me he considered Mr. Finlayson one of the best officers in the department.

I was not attempting in
any way to criticize Mr. Finlayson. I have no reason to have anything else but respect for him. But I notice at page 85 of the Estimates of 1924, that is two years ago, the Superintendent of Insurance was granted $1,000 additional to his salary. Can the minister tell me what Mr. Finlayson's salary was in 1924?
No.

If the minister will look, he will find that two years ago he increased what the statute allowed, from $5,000 to $6,000. by the simple expedient of a vote in the estimates. This last year, not content with that increase, he put through a vote of $5;000, replacing the $1,000 increase, and making the salary $10,000, or twice the amount the statute allowed. That has continued this year. As to Mr. Finlayson's ability I have not the least doubt in the world. He is not only a resourceful man, but he is an exceedingly determined and self-willed man.

Is not that a pretty good
type to have in the department?
It is, but like everything else it requires restraint.
We all require that.

I do not see it applied
very much, though.
Some require a rope.

A rope would not do
much harm here. I am sure I have given the history of it correctly. Now this excuse about the insurance companies wanting him
paid this much because they pay it, is just so much air, so much froth and eyewash. Insurance companies, of course, have a large scale of salaries, and the men in that business have not very much difficulty in getting them. It is all passed on. But a little excess passed on to the public is reflected in a pretty big way in the central office.. I suppose they like working in with the department, but the fact is that the public has got to pay it. It all comes down ultimately to the public; they have to pay the money. I do not know any reason in the world why a man carrying out the provisions of a statute, even though I think it has been unnecessarily enlarged, in the way of a supervisor, with no duty of making any money, no responsibility of making a real commercial success of it, differing in that way wholly from the responsibility that is centered on the head of an individual business, should get in a class like this and thereby contribute to raising the whole level of salaries in the country, when the country is going back, as it undoubtedly is, one hundred million dollars a year. If there is any method in the world of preventing any further increase in the general scale in any way at all, it ought to be done; it has got to be done. But I do not know when the opposite tendency was more accentuated than it has been this last two or three years. I do not doubt the ministers could point to some importunity to which they have not yielded, but they would have difficulty, I think. One deputy minister after another came in first, under one classification; then they got in under another classification, because there were some left out of the first, until finally the whole of them got intend drew $8,000. Those immediately under them are creeping into close approach, and the superintendent of insurance sets a grand example when he goes up to $10,000. This is all fine for everybody except the taxpayer of Canada.

I would like to call the
minister's attention to the fact that a salary of $10,000 is equal to the salary of any judicial position in Canada with the exception of the salaries on the bench of the Supreme Court of Canada. It is therefore rather extraordinary in the line of salaries. I have a very great admiration for the ability as well as the persistency of the gen'leman who is receiving the salary, but I want to emphasize, if I may, the fact that it is the practice cf governments throughout the country to think that in some way they escape criticism, or in fact escape responsibility, by devolving upon some groups or associations a part
Supply-Finance

of the public charge. I know in the provinces i is a common thing to say: Oh well, we have imposed such and such a tax upon people in a certain line of business; therefore the public does not bear it, and it is no expenditure on the part of the government. The same thing is being said here. It is not healthy. We cannot expect any charge to be put upon any department of business without having that charge reflected in the cost of that business to the people. If you take insurance, while it is competitive in a sense, we all know the rates are absolutely fixed, and necessarily fixedi, by agreement between the companies. Therefore, every penny that you add to the cost of administering the insurance system as a whole must be reflected in the rates charged the people for their insurance. It is not much use to talk about the high ccst of living when by one little step after another we do everything in our power to enhance the cost of the different things that go to make up a living.

Has the
minister received any reports from the Inspector General of Banks this year?

That does not come under
this vote, but I may say that I have received a number of reports from him. I receive reports from him every week.

In further reference to
Mr. Finlayson's salary, just to set the matter right I sent out to the library for the statutes, and I find that by chapter 29 of 7-8 Edward VII:
The Governor in Council may appoint an officer to be called the Superintendent of Insurance. . . . and such officer shall be paid suc(J salary, not exceeding five thousand dollars per annum, as the Governor in Council, may, from time to time, fix and determine.
That is his original salary was not to exceed $5,000. It does not say it has to be up to $5,000, but it must not exceed that figure. So since 1908 this man's salary has doubled. I would be the last to protest against paying to a decent extent any civil servant, but we must not forget that when we are paying a civil servant a salary of $10,000, that is as good as S15.000 a year to a professional man. Take a doctor, or a lawyer, more particularly, because a lawyer has mere expense. He would have to earn $15,000, which is a pretty fair income in Canada for the ordinary lawyer .or doctor, to make $10,000 a year net. I only mention this in a general way so far as I am concerned, but I wish to associate myself with the others who have protested against any general increase of salaries at this time, when we should be endeavouring to cut them 
down instead of increasing them. If in 190a we could get a man for $5,000 while the cost of living may have risen it has not increased to the extent of justifying the doubling of a man's salary.

In regard to this particular
officer, my own feeling is that Mr. Finlayson is entitled to as much salary as the other deputy ministers, but I do deplore very much the increases in the salaries of the deputy ministers that have taken place in the last three years. I do not see any justification for it. I have spoken on this matter in previous years. I think it has been a great mistake to have had such large and rapid increases in the salaries of deputy ministers.

Item agreed to.
To provide for the expenses of work in the interest of fire prevention to be carried on by the Department of Insurance, $10,000.

I should like to know just what is being done in connection with this vote? In some of the provinces it has become the custom now to have a local officer appointed to investigate the causes of fire. It has been done in my own province, and I think the results are good. I should like to know in a general way just how this money is spent, through whom, and the genera! character of the expenditure?

This vote is for fire prevention purposes. The amount is $10,000 as compared with $12,000 for 1924-25. The vote includes the salary of Mr. J. Grove Smith $4,800 and of Miss B. N. Grafton senior clerk-stenographer, $1,440. The expenditure for 1921-22 was $10,680.51; for 1922-23 $18,287.37; and for 1923-24, $11,380.70. The expenses during the current fiscal year were:	salaries
$6,164.67, travelling $1,059.09. printing $1,737.55, sundries $463.67; total $9,549.49.

I wonder if the minister
realizes that, listening to him as well as I could, I have got the idea that this vote costs the country a little less than $10,000 this year; that it consisted in salaries to Mr. A., Miss B. and some other people, and some travelling expenses. After that explanation I am left just as much in the dark as ever as to what those people do. I do not doubt that some people got salaries, but I want to know, if I can, and if the minister has the information, in what practical way these people are doing anything that results in any benefit to the country. I assume they are doing something, but I want to know what it is.

Supply-Finance

Mr. J. Grove Smith is sent
about investigating fires, wherever they take place, and giving lectures urging people to do what they can to prevent fires. In a word he is carrying on fire prevention work. I understand that in addition to that the officials have had under consideration for some, time- and they claim they will complete the work this year-some experiments in connection with fireproof roofing. The idea is to demonstrate to the people how best to prevent fires; and those who desire it can get information as to the proper construction in order to get the lowest insurance rates.

I am getting a little more
interested. I think I remember now hearing something about the fireproof material last year. It surely cannot take very long to determine the qualities of that material. Some of these investigations remind me a good deal of something that happened down in my home town some years ago. There had been extensive dredging done by Canada. Then some people drove piling into the sloping bank. Then they put a wharf on top of the piling and were preparing to put a warehouse on top of the wharf in the full faith that the laws of nature would be suspended in favour of the port of St. John. They were not, however, and the whole thing toppled over into the water. Then they brought engineers in-very skilled men standing high in their profession. One of them took some mud and put it in a tea cup with some water and stirred it round in order to determine what the cause of the accident was. Any longshoreman, or any person of ordinary observation would have told him the cause of what had 'happened. I think if some of these Laurier matches that are supplied around this House were properly scratched and applied to a bit of so-called fireproof material, it would resolve the question in a very few seconds as to whether it was fireproof or not. So far as that goes the minister's explanation has really not impressed me to any extent, except with the idea that somebody is getting a salary, or that several people are to do something that I do not see has yet resulted in any particular benefit. Now, lectures are being delivered. Are these lectures delivered to insurance companies or to the general -public, and if so, at what points are they given and what is the net result of them?
I know what is 'being done in my own province with the money that is being spent there for fire protection. I know the fire marshal.
I know that he holds investigations. I know that he makes reports as to the causes of " 266
fire, and I know that he institutes prosecutions. I am only speaking as a member of the public; I have no special source of information apart from the newspapers. But the minister who asks for this vote has not yet told me a single definite thing that is being done by these people. This is a small amount, it is true, but it seems to me it is something someone has started, and in another form is adding to the high cost of living without giving the slightest bit of benefit. I am driven to that conclusion for the want of any better explanation.

I have not the details of all the activities of this gentleman during the year. If my hon. friend would get the report of the Department of Insurance he might find something there; but when he said that I have not yet impressed him I wonder if I can impress him with this talk: this work was started in 1921 and we have reduced the expenditure from $18,287.37 to $9,549.49. I wonder if that impresses my hon. friend?
Why not abolish it altogether?
I suggested that myself.
I would agree with you.

I made inquiry when this
question came up before the Treasury board and asked why this expenditure should be made. It was represented to me that this man was doing some good work, and they wanted him kept in office at least until they had completed the investigation into fireproofing material which was under way and which is taken care of by another vote, to be reached in a few minutes.
Is not this officer one of the staff that was shelved from the Conservation Commission?
I could not say.

I think if the minister investigates the history of this official he will find that he was one of the former staff of the Conservation Commission. As far as I can learn nearly every one of those gentlemen has been provided for in some other branch of the service. I think the minister's impulse when he made his inquiry before the Treasury board was a proper one. As far as investigation into fires is concerned, that is being conducted now by the Board of Underwriters in every province. In the province of New Brunswick, as my hon. friend

Supply-Finance

(Mr. Baxter) pointed out, they have appointed fire marshals, who make a very searching inquiry into every fire that occurs in that province, in many instances there have been prosecutions, and in some cases convictions, following their activities. That I think is the greatest deterrent of fire that we can have in the shape of legislation, and it really is a work that should be done by the provinces, being a matter purely of civil rights. I suggest to the minister to strike out this vote.

I would not like to strike it out now, but I am glad to have this criticism, because it is not.far out, from my own observation, when it came before the Treasury board. I do not know Grove Smith. I only met him once in Vancouver just after the great fire in British Columbia. I recall that he had been sent up there to go into that matter and see if he could not stir up enthusiasm to have something done to prevent these fires.

Then probably his work
has been of some value. What is the minister's opinion as to the activities of the provincial governments in this matter? With the exception of certain portions of the country, these lands are owned by provincial governments and they are very much alive to the question of fire protection and have spent a good deal of money. I do not think there is the slightest criticism of these expenditures, provided the money is well expended, and I would suggest having this item eliminated.
Not this trip.

This practice started in
1921, and the suggestion was that it was done by the predecessors of the present government.
Oh, no.

I do not care about that, because I think they were capable of making mistakes, and I think perhaps this is one. If the present government does not make any more serious mistakes I do not object. But the minister will note every year there are millions of dollars worth of practically irreplaceable material in the natural resources of the country going up in smoke. The provinces that are interested in timber are doing a great deal. They have not been able- and perhaps no one ever will be-to cope successfully with this destruction by fire, but fMr. HansonJ
this amount of money is too small to save even the dwelling houses or the timber. It would be far better to turn this money into another channel, put more with it and do something to save our natural resources. In other words if we are spending the money, spend. enough to do some good.

Item agreed to.
To provide for the expenses of a technical investigation under the supervision of the Department of Insurance into the merits of the various forms of roof coverings from the standpoint of fire protection, $8,000.

I thought the last vote
covered this.

No. The last item was to provide for watching this matter for the department. This work is carried on in the laboratory in McGill University under the direction of Professor French, Mr. Mackay and Mr. Johnson. Mr. J. Grove Smith is the link between the department and this work.

I suppose the first vote we passed was to pay for the man who held the match and scratched it, and this is to pay the man who looked at the result. As a matter of commonsense, can it be contended that it takes more than two successive 9 p.m.. years to find out about every roof covering we have in this country, and that it costs $8,000 odd to find out what will burn and what will not burn. I sympathize with the minister. He has had this thing loaded upon him. It is part of the precedent, and he can never get rid of it.

I think this will be the last
year.
I hope it will be.
I am sure it will be.

How many years has this
vote been running?

The record I have does not
go back any further than the previous year, when the amount was $8,500. It is down to $8,000 now. This is only the second year for this grant.

Mr. HANSO'N:	I think we should have a
general statement from the minister as to the activities of the past year and the prospects for the future. There is a great deal of criticism of this department with regard to its activities and lack of results.

The reduction of $70,000 is
the result of a decrease of ninety-six in the number of temporary employees throughout our immigration service, whose salaries have been paid out of this vote for a number of years. In 1924-25 we had 170 temporary employees and for 1925-26 we have reduced this number to seventy-four only, or a decrease of ninety-six. There are 82 positions which will be permanent appointments. This permanent reorganization has been effected with the approval of the Civil Service Commission. To cover the salaries of these eighty-two the amount of $50,000 will be provided for in the supplementary estimates for 1925-26 under the heading of immigration outside service salaries. The net result of this reorganization will therefore be: (a) A net reduction of fourteen in the number of our outside service employees; (b) a net decrease or saving of $20,000 in salaries.

What was the reason of the
$229,000 reduction last year?
We are getting along with less money. That is the reason.

Is that the only reason you
can give?

How many immigrants
were brought in during the last fiscal year?

In 1924-25 there were 111,362
and the year before 148,560.

There is a very marked
falling off in immigration into this country. I take it that this total includes not only immigrants from Europe but also those from 266i	:
the United States. We are voting each year a large sum of money for immigration purposes and the results are extremely disappointing. The minister should be prepared to make a general statement covering the whole field of activities of the department when he asks parliament to pass a vote of this kind. The government is asking for a blank cheque of some $1,350,000 to be disposed of by order in council just as it may see fit, and that is rather a large order in these days. The minister therefore owes it to himself as well as to the House and the country to give some more satisfactory explanation than we have so far received. As a matter of fact we have not yet had any explanation. What is the policy of the government?

To be frank, the policy of
the government is to secure quality rather than quantity. We are careful in the admission of citizens to bring in such people as we believe will remain in Canada, and we are more particularly interested in the type of people who will settle on the land and stay there. We are also endeavouring as far as possible to bring in families. When you bring -in a single man who has no ties he has no anchor to keep him on the land and he is more apt to drift away. This is not so in the case of the family unit, and for this reason we endeavour to bring in families. The difficulties to-day are greater than those that had to be met some years ago. In the first place, Canada has no free lands to offer as she had at that time, when we were prepared to give 160 acres to anyone who would settle. We have not that free land to-day, although land is available at reasonable prices. These are some of the difficulties so far as Canada itself is concerned. And in the United Kingdom and elsewhere on the continent the people have not as much money as they had before and consequently are unable to travel. The conditions are worse in Europe now than they- have ever been before, and they are worse than they are in Canada. The governments of those countries are not anxious to part with the agricultural type that we require. Then the cost of transportation is higher; it costs a family of five $580 to come to Canada to-day. This of course is a considerable drain on the capital with which the immigrant starts out. A few years ago the same family could come to Canada for $165. These are some of the difficulties which the department is actively engaged in overcoming. The number of immigrants coming in from the United States is however larger than heretofore; I refer to the agri
Supply-Immigration

cultural type. Favourable prices for the products of the farm will do more to induce the people to come into the country than all the missionary lecturers whom you could send abroad could accomplish. The people will go where they see an opportunity to improve their position in life. I am bound to say that there has been a good deal of adverse criticism of this country disseminated by the press of other countries. We are receiving letters every day from Canadians both at home and abroad who want to know why we do not take some steps to stop the propaganda, particularly in the press of the United States, against this country. We are doing all we can to counteract such criticism and we are getting more favourable publicity now. But we may as well admit frankly that Canada has received very unfavourable advertising from "whispers of death" and the lamentations of Jeremiahs out of office published in Canadian newspapers and magazines and reproduced in the press of the Old World. And every member of parliament who gets up in this House and puts on the records of parliament criticism adverse to this country is helping to injure Canada. It is well to criticize a government, but there is a limit. There is a difference between criticizing the government and running down your country, and Canada is suffering from that sort of thing just now. However, I believe that conditions are improving in this respect and there is less of this sort of thing now than two years ago or so. I am not without hopes that if we can secure more reasonable transportation rates *there will foe a tide of immigration to the *land which will produce revenues for the railways; because every man who produces agricultural commodities adds to the business available for the railways. The policy of the government is to have a selective type of immigration, more particularly of people who will go on the land and remain there.

The minister's statement is an absolute confession of failure on the part of the government to put into effect any policy of immigration that would produce' results. The figures he has given to-night speak more eloquently than any words I could utter of that failure. We find a decrease of 37,198 as compared with the year before. Let me tell the minister that no one in this corner of the House has been running down the fair name of Canada. We have not decried the country but rather have we tried to stand behind it. What we have said is that the country is cursed with an inefficient government on the treasury benches.

Mr. ROBB; My hon. friend protests too much.

The minister cannot point to any words of mine that are derogatory of this country. We have simply pointed out that an inefficient government is now in office, and the minister's statement to-night is a sufficient indication that after four years in office the government has absolutely failed in the direction of immigration. The minister speaks of a selected type of immigrant. That might be all right if there was not such a crying need for population in this country. I suggest to the minister that any white man or white woman willing to work ought to be welcome. We need them.
What for?
To fill up the vacant spaces, to do the work of this country.

How many jobs can you
give them?

The hon member for
Quebec West (Mr. Parent) can make his own speech when the time arrives.
I will, right after you finish.

The results so far show an absolute failure on the part of the government to measure up to the requirements of the times. The railways of this country are doing ten times as much as the government in immigration work, and I suspect that there is a tremendous lot of duplication of effort by the railway agencies and the government. The minister ought to co-ordinate the work of these agencies with the activities of his own department so that we may have effective results. Canada is a good country-there are lots of opportunities here for people who are willing to work. The difficulty to-day is that many people do not want to work. That class is not needed here. But it ought not to be difficult for Canada to get immigrants in competition with Australia. From what I can read I gather that the sister dominion is outstripping us at every turn. I am aware that there has been a certain amount of propaganda against Canada. I happened to have the privilege of reading a couple of letters that appeared recently in the Yorkshire Post, written ostensibly from Canada, and I understood that the government was endeavouring to ascertain their authorship. I wonder if they have succeeded in tracing the origin of this propaganda. It seemed to me that the fair name of the Dominion has been defamed, and that it should be the business of the department to trace the propaganda to its source and, if possible, stamp it out.

Supply-Immigration

Mr. Chairman, when this
vote was up about a month ago I was told by the very courteous and fair minister (Mr. Robb) that the House would later on be given an opportunity to discuss the whole question of what I wanted then to discuss-migration within the empire. This is the second if not the first largest problem Canada has to solve, yet during the past four and a half months we have devoted only about two and a half hours to its discussion. What is wrong with Canada? How are we to account for the small growth of our population during the past twenty years? These two questions are on everybody's lips in the Mother Country today. Australia is catching up with us and will soon be ahead in this respect. Indeed, it has been predicted by a prominent cabinet minister of Great Britain that within the next seventy-five years Australia will have a population of one hundred million if not surpassing the United States. The trouble with this country is that during probably the last twenty-five years we have followed the policy of laissez faire and let well enough alone in immigration, and the estimates for the current year for immigration are comparatively about the same as they were a quarter of a century ago.
The greatest problem of the British Empire to-day is to redistribute its population. Many returned soldiers among the two and a half million out of work who are to-day receiving doles in England would make the very best class of settlers in the overseas dominions. I agree with the resolution which has been passed by many of the church organizations throughout the country. At the recent synod of the, Anglican church of Canada, His Grace the Primate of Canada supported this resolution, which was carried:
That this council expresses its very strong conviction that at the present juncture a decided preference should be given to immigrants from the British Isles.
I believe that the opinion throughout Canada to-day is that these British immigrants who are our own kith and kin, make the very finest settlers, and I am confident that we would get many more of them if there was less red tape in the administration of the depialrtmejntA On this ipoint the following article in the Empire Magazine for February by Mr. Obed Smith is interesting:
Then again the system has become overburdened with red-tape. The recruiting sergeant in the field cannot sign on a man without first consulting the war office. I know of a case, a splendid farmer candidate in Scotland who has been kept waiting since September having his case investigated at Ottawa. In the meantime he cannot give notice on the farm he is occupying. He may be lost through delay.
Is it by accident or design that during the past few years the proportion of British to other immigrants has been roughly about 35 or 45 per cent to 65 or 55?
If the figures you quote are accurate, I should say it is not by design. The highest years' figure I remember was before the war about 400,000. Of them 150,000 were from Great Britain. At present immigration is declining steadily, 1924 less than 1923, and 1925, so far, less than corresponding months last year. Great apathy is shown. Of the three million pounds set aside by Great Britain for assistance in overseas settlement only four hundred thousand have been claimed by all the Dominions together. That is certainy not getting together in the right spirit to fill the waste spaces.
Cannot more be done in the way of community settlement? It seems to me that the greatest obstacle to settling people from thickly populated areas in large open spaces is the loneliness of the life.
I have always contended that the Homesteading Act was wrong in compelling homesteaders to reside on part of their holdings. They would be much happier in small communities on land set apart for that purpose, houses within easy reach, a small store or two, a blacksmith shop, a wireless set and some attempt to bring about a community spirit. It would go a long way to alleviate the trials of the western settler. It was such community co-operation which made the Doukhobor settlements so prosperous.
Suppose I am an English country-born man, with a family, and have scraped together 50 or 100 pounds, wbat can I get in Canada for it?
You must first make application to the London office. Then someone is sent out to interview you and your wife and members of your family. Particulars are sent to Ottawa, and if approved, you are sent to the part of Canada you are deemed most suitable to. You are given a farm for which you must pay in 25 years. You will be found some chickens and a cow perhaps, and will be expected to hire out to get some local knowledge of farming. Your wife and family meantime will exist on the farm allotted to you. You will also be given a loan by the government.
And if the farm is not consdered suitable by me?
Then you can go somewhere else, but at your own expense.
Does not the system seem rather vague and discouraging to the settler, even if he is willing to work?
You cannot give him too much preference, else you are up against the farmers' sons already settled and wishing to take up land about him.
I want to refer to what has been said by some leaders of thought in this country with regard to this subject. The Prime Minister of Canada recently stated:
If we cease our efforts to fill those great wast8 spaces with working and productive units, Canada is destined to lag behind and fail to realize what should be her future.
The late Lord Shaughnessy said:
That the vital importance of Canada's future lay in a sound, sane immigration policy, to be promulgated immediately and to be carried out with intelligence and vigour.
His successor, my distinguished Canadian friend, Mr. E. W. Beatty, president of the. Canadian Pacific Railway Company, said last January:
Seasonal or other unemployment should not have a direct influence on such a national question as immigration. One of the surest ways to avoid unemployment would be the presence in the country of more productive units, whose necessities would mean greater consumption, more activity, and therefore more employment.
