ferent parts of the empire. It shows how our votes rose by small amounts from $1,300,000 to $1,500,000, $1,800,000 and $2,000,000 last year; and that has been only slightly increased this year. Out of four hundred millions for Canada's government only two millions have been spent on immigration this year. I had intended to speak in the debate a month ago but the minister has very generously given me an opportunity of laying these few facts before the House on this occasion, by one who desires to see our great empire grow and expand. Nearly all of our ancestors came from the British isles.

I like the spirit of my hon.
friend from North Toronto (Mr. Church). I am bound to say I think it would be better for Canada if all the members of parliament, no matter how much they might criticize the government, would lose no opportunity of saying a good word for their own country and point out, as my hon. friend from North Toronto says, that there are opportunities here for those who are willing to work, opportunities equal to any that are to be found in our sister Dominions.
Mr. hon. friend has quoted some figures regarding the migration of Britishers from British Isles to the several overseas Dominions, and has expressed regret that the number going to Australia, New Zealand and South Africa is far beyond the number of those coming to Canada. But let me point out that the conditions are somewhat different. For instance, in the case of married families going to Australia, two-thirds of the passage is paid, one-tturd by the government of the United Kingdom, and one-third by the government of Australia, and for domestics going to Australia, the whole fare is paid. Those conditions do not apply to Canada.

What are
the conditions here?

We make advances by way
of loans, and the money is afterwards refunded?	-

Did not
the British government, under the British Umpire Settlement Act advance the total cost of passages for immigrants so far as Canada was concerned?
No.

What was
the arrangement?
Why not do something towards getting immigrants on the land when we get them here?

The minister has stated
that for the year mentioned 63,016 passengers came to Canada and 38,599 went to Australia. Well, I venture to make the assertion that out of the 38,599 that went to Australia a much larger proportion of them will remain in Australia than remained in Canada after they came here.

Where could those who
*went to Australia go?

That, perhaps, affords a
partial explanation; but the difficulty in the case of Canada is to keep the immigrants here after they arrive. I know that in the summer, when I was at home, at different times I was inundated with requests from British born citizens-the very finest type of citizens that a country could have-asking me for certificates of health to permit them to go to the United States.

Was that after your speech
on the budget?

No, it was not after my
speech on the budget. My hon. friend, though, has profited by it. He knows that if he made a speech he would drive them out altogether.

They are coming across in
thousands now.

They are not immigrants,
they are only transients.
They are crossing for irrigation purposes.

They do not need to go
as far as Windsor for irrigation purposes; they can get irrigation in such sections even as Ottawa I understand. But the point I was trying to make is that we should endeavour, as well as we can, to hold immigrants here when we get them, and I suggest that the government should make greater efforts than in the past to cure the unemployment condition here in order to keep them in the country.

Does my hon. friend
know-I think this can be verified by the records if we had a little time-that the net increase in population in Australia last year was about 5,000? In other words there was emigration from Australia too which offset the immigration so as to cause a net gain of 5,000. I think I can get the data and figures from my office to prove that statement to my hon. friend.
What was the net decrease in Canada?
My hon. friends opposite have argued that point to their satisfaction on several occasions, although I think their figures were a little off colour.

I do not think it will make much difference what any of us has to say on this question of immigration. We have discussed it- at some length not only this year but in previous years. I am quite sure that even if I were to offer some advice to the minister he would not take it-
Do not be too sure.

And if he did take it perhaps it would not solve the immigration problem to his satisfaction. I notice that the government, through the minister, is very anxious to blame every one else but themselves for a result for which they are more responsible than any other person or group of persons in the dominion. I wish to follow the example of the hon. member for York-Sunbury (Mr. Hanson) in repudiating the charge, that I have said anything in this House, or anywhere else against the good name of Canada. I do not think it would make much difference if I did, providing that there were no real grounds for adverse criticism1. On the other hand, we are asked by the minister to speak a good word for our country. I think the good things in Canada do not need advertising. That is true of all countries. I think the country about the goodness of which people have to be howling all the time is not a very good country. If we have to stand here and protest our goodness it is unlikely that w,e shall produce a very great effect on anybody else. Surely the government can distinguish-I am sure the people outside can-between the criticism which we offer against the policy of the government as it affects the economic life of the nation, and criticism of Canada as a nation having regard to the resources of the country and the desirability of this Dominion as a home for immigrants under ordinary cir-
Supply-Immigration

cumstances. There is surely a very wide distinction between those two questions, >and I do not think the Minister of Immigration can find one single instance on Hansard or anywhere else where I have even suggested that Canada was not indeed a very great country, a very rich country, and a very excellent country in which to live. We all are aware of the extent of our territory. The actual natural wealth of the country is a subject for poetical eloquence, and I notice often hon gentlemen opposite indulge in it. Certainly we have immeasurable wealth; there is no doubt about that; and there is lots of room We are all aware that if we had a family of five on every half section in western Canada we would, by that very fact, very materially improve all public services and reduce their cost. We know perfectly well that if we could increase the population of Canada by another nine millions next year we would cut in half the per capita debt of the country and by increase in traffic be able to reduce freight rates. These would all be desirable things and would probably result were our population so increased. We are all aware of these things, and we know that Canada can accommodate very many more *millions of people than we have in the country at present. These are all common facts and everybody knows them. There is no need to state them, but when we have said all that, it is surely a very serious commentary on the administration that we cannot hold nine million of people and keep them well fed in a country so vast, so rich in resources and so good. That is the commentary and I lay it at the door of the Minister of Immigration and his government. That is the criticism I make.
What is the remedy?

The remedy, and one which my hon. friend would not like to follow, is partly to secure a new government. I told my hon. friend ait the ov.lset that if I offered some advice it would not be accepted. But that is part of the advice I would give now -either a new government or else a good deal more wisdom and initiative in the government we have. So far as that is concerned, I am not particular about throwing out this government or any other government. What I want to see is intelligent action, I do not care which government takes such action. I want to point out that we are not getting the best for the money we are expending on immigration, and in making that comment I want it to be clearly understood again that I am not speaking against immigration under

all conditions. I am only speaking against immigration under the specific conditions in which we are placed at the present time. I consider that we are not getting the best for the money we are expending on immigration. The first reason for that is that we no sooner bring these people into the country than they go out. Surely that is not a good investment. Will the minister say that these people went out because the hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Garland) made a speech in this House? Will he say they went out because some other hon. member made a speech in this House? He will not say that. He will say they went out-if he states what he actually knows in his heart-because this administration failed to find work and sustenance for them after bringing them in. That is why they went out. If the problem of finding work for Canadian citizens is beyond the government, let them say so and we will stop criticizing. If it is outside the sphere of politics, make it known to the people of Canada, but if it can reasonably be done by any government why does this government not do it? These people are going out. Why is the government finding it difficult to keep them in Canada? Let us suppose that 10,000 people who went from Canada to the United States last year, wrote 10,000 letters to their friends in Great Britain and said to them, "We came to Canada; we were there for so many weeks, we got nothing to do, funds became short and we moved into the United States. We have now work to perform, and we would advise you, if you are going to cross the Atlantic, to come this way." That is something like the letters which would be written. Does the minister blame the hon. member for Bow River for that? Is that blame not more befitting the government?
The minister has not blamed the hon. member for Bow River this year; he might do so.
I had an idea that he had it in his mind that that was the man who ought to be blamed.
That is the most unkindest cut of all.

I do not know of any hon.
member who is more fearlessly honest in his portrayal of western life than the hon. member for Bow River.
I would not blame any hon. member in this connection. Hon. members have simply stated the facts in regard to the situation.
The next reason why we are not getting the best for the money is that apparently the

minister is having a difficult task in inducing people from Great Britain to come here, after what they have heard from the people who have gone to the United States. You cannot blame any member of this House or anybody else for that. Does the minister think that hon. members of this House are talking just to hear their voices?-although many of them no doubt like that very much. After about six months we get tired of even that. Those of us who oppose the immigration policy of the government are not so anxious to hear our voices. We really think there is something in what we are saying. I have in my hand, for instance, a poster published by the Unemployed Association of Canada, and this Unemployed Association has sent this all over the British Empire and perhaps, over the entire world for all I know. They state here that they are undertaking to collect certain statistics, and if they secure these statistics and send them out I would not be surprised if nobody came to Canada at all next year. This may be a very unpatriotic thing to do, but they are doing it, and why?
Because they are no good.
The noble Daniel from the western mountains tells us they are no good.
He is the gentleman with the big income tax.

He has settled the matter. That is very much like what the government does. The government says the people from Great Britain who will not come here at our call are the people we do not want. The people who come here and get tired are neople who are no good and do not want to work. Seemingly no people are any good, because we cannot get any of them to come here or to stay.	*
I do not want to prick my hon. friend's argument-
Which one and with what?
With actual facts.
Has the hon. member got one fact?

I want to tell the hon.
member that under the laws that exist in the United States no one who comes from Great Britain can go there except under their quota or two per cent law. The only people who are admitted are Canadian bom citizens; so that those people who go there are Canadian born and their places are taken by those who come from Europe.

There is an underground
railway running strongly all through the country. If my hon. friend doubts me I will have him come down to New Brunswick and I will show him the route.
What is the date of that resolution?
It bears no date.

I was wondering whether it
coincided with the date on which, a delegation waited upon Premier Greenfield of Alberta requesting work. He found work for them and only seven or eight would take it, and he told them to get out because there was nothing to keep them in Edmonton if they were not willing to work.

I am not sure whether the date of this resolution synchronizes with the event to which the minister refers. But in any case the suggestion the minister advances that there is no unemployment is too utterly unreasonable to merit a reply. It is so ridiculous that I refuse to take up the time of the committee discussing it. It is true no doubt that here and there you will find men who, for mental or physical reasons, are unable to work. But that fact does not explain the general unemployment situation. Now, I want to make it clear that this circular is the kind of thing that is preventing the minister's immigration policy from being a success; and the thing to do is not to stop these people from sending resolutions of this sort away but to alter the conditions that make such resolutions necessary. That is where the responsibility falls on the minister and on the government.
I believe that the money which it is proposed to spend this year on immigration could be of far greater service to Canada if it were expended in Nova Scotia. The minister cannot prevent the situation in Nova Scotia from becoming known not only throughout the British Empire but throughout the world at large; nor can the minister blame any individual member of this House for the propaganda which is being broadcast in that connection. That sore has been festering for many years and every member of 'the House knows the 'gravity of the situation as it exists to-day. Still nothing is being done. I maintain therefore that if the government would spend this amount or half of it in Nova Scotia to get the industry of that part of the country going and to enable the men to co-operate with their employers in the production of coal and steel, it would be a far better advertisement for this country, in the eyes of people who might be inclined to cotme here, than sending out some missionary, as the minister says, to Glasgow or London or anywhere else to try to inveigle people into coming here.

I am willing to admit that the economic conditions in Canada to-day are no worse than they are in Great Britain or that obtain in many countries; but granting that does not help the unemployment any. It seems to me rather a shame to allow any family of five poor working people to pay $580 to cross the Atlantic from Glasgow or London when perhaps they have nothing to do when they come here. I should like to know what the initial investment would amount to for a family of five going on the land in Canada. When you take into consideration their fares, the house in which they must live, the price of the land, the price of implements, and provisions for the first year's grub, and what interest is being charged. I do, not doubt that these people and their children will be kept busy as long as they live, paying interest to those who lend them the necessary money with which to start. These are the conditions under which immigrants are coming in. I need not weary the committee with a recital of the facts which they already know as well as I do, if not better. In reviewing the situation, looking at our vast natural resources, our plant and equipment, and the capacity for producing wealth, I am reminded of the old superstitious lines of doggerel which declare that "every prospect pleases and only man is vile." I disagree with that as philosophy, but I agree with it as applied to the present administration. I do not mean to suggest of course that the administration is vile in the sense intended in this line; but considering the manner in which it has disregarded its responsibility in this matter the lines are apropos. There are opportunities for the development of our vast natural resources and of building a nation of happy and prosperous citizens, but the government i3 not taking advantage of these opportunities. I would offer a suggestion to the minister, and I do so only because I believe that he has a spark of genius if only he would allow himself to put it to some use, The very best thing that Canada could do to attract immigrants from any part of the world would be to give full scope to the genius of real statesmanship and to compel a country as rich in resources as this is to yield more than a bare living to nine millions of a population.

Notwithstanding
what the minister (Mr. Robb) has said, I believe there are a good many people in this Dominion who still have confidence that there is a bright future in store for Canada. I know that a great many build those hopes on the great natural resources of our country and

the expectation of a great influx of immigration from other countries to fill up the vacant spaces and utilize the equipment which we have provided at a great cost for a population much larger than that we now have. But I am afraid that the government itself is not very hopeful so far as the near future is concerned. There is no question that the cost of government in this country, federal, provincial, municipal and otherwise, has increased enormously during the past few years, and it is a grievous burden on the people. There is in connection with immigration a duplication, the aggregate result of which ought to show better results if we were getting anything like value for the money expended. I am not sure what policy the government has in mind. At the last session of parliament a committee of the House was appointed to consider the question of old age pensions, and I have almost come to the conclusion, in view of the fact that there is a reduction of $300,000 in this item, that the government intends to adopt a system of old age pensions in Canada as an inducement to people to come here and in this way hold them here. The Canadian Pacific Railway Company last ' year, according to their financial statement, spent $758,510 on colonization and immigration work. The Canadian National Railways spent $770,454 for the same purpose. In fact, this other branch of government increased its expenditure by nearly $400,000 over the previous year. Some of the provincial governments are also doing a great deal of work along this line. There must be something absolutely and radically wrong or better results would follow. The fault does not rest with the country, notwithstanding the criticism of the minister. I do not think there is anyone who will not stand up and stoutly maintain that Canada possesses natural resources unequalled, or at least unsurpassed, by any other country in the world.
Hear, hear.

I do not think the
sun shines upon a country that offers greater natural inducements for the willing worker than does this Dominion. But with all our great natural advantages we are labouring under certain artificial handicaps that must be removed before we will have a satisfactory condition of affairs. The minister referred to the efforts put forth to induce immigrants to go on the land and to keep them there. Why all this anxiety about confining them to the land? It would be much better to have these people employed in our own cities than
to have them employed in the industrial centres in foreign countries manufacturing goods for our consumption and use. It is well known that the great exodus from our rural districts is chiefly into our towns and cities. And it is quite natural that the people should go where they find the best opportunities. You may talk until you are blind, but you cannot convince those who know better than you do that they are making a mistake. They know what they are doing. Our people are intelligent, and there is no use preaching the doctrine, "Oh, you are foolish, you will do much better on the land than you will in the urban centres." That doctrine has been preached so long that it is now threadbare. I repeat, there is something radically wrong, or conditions such as we now have would not prevail.
Reference has been made to emigration to Australia. Australia is in a different position to Canada. They are not living alongside the most energetic and progressive nation in the world, a nation that has adopted a fiscal policy which is bound to have a tremendous influence upon the course this Dominion is compelled to take. We cannot escape that influence if we wished to, and we might much better realize that now and deal with an imperative necessity as at any other time. In the main our fiscal policy will always be dictated by that of our great neighbours to the south of us. We know full well that many of the best of our people have crossed the line during the past few years, and are now residents of the United States. The greatest loss we have sustained since the Great war has been this exodus of native-born Canadians to the United States.
I admit that it is necessary to establish proper safeguards against the entry of an undesirable class of people, people who congregate in our big cities and who neither know how to work, nor intend to do honest labour. We have altogether too many of that class at present. But a reduction of $300,000 in these estimates is rather significant in view of the fact that it is so seldom that we find a reduction of any consequence in any of the other estimates. Why have not the government applied the pruning knife to a lot of this deadwood that might well be cut out? For two at least of the items that were passed a few minutes ago the minister stated he did not believe there was any justification; yet they were passed.

But my hon. friend will at
least give me credit for having reduced the estimates of the Department of Finance by $70,000?

On the whole the reductions made are very slight, and I think by the time the supplementary estimates are brought down it will be found that those reductions have been more than offset. Now, we have a system that to my mind is rather disturbing; that is, we have a privileged class which is continually increasing in number. I refer to those engaged in the civil service of this country. I do not intend to cast the slightest reflection upon the ability of those people, because if there is any class in the Dominion which has my heartfelt sympathy it is the civil service. Many young people entertain the idea that if they can only become attached to the civil service they are going to be happy for the rest of their days, and immediately they succeed they find that their initiative is destroyed, there is but little opportunity for expansion, or development, and finally they become reconciled to the situation and say, "Oh, well, what's the use? We may just as well drift along with the crowd." The hours of labour for the civil service have been fixed within certain limits; the rate of wages has also been fixed. Since the Canadian National Railways came under this category there has been an enormous addition to the civil service. An increase of over 100,000 with this result. If you are living in the country and wish to do some business in shipping on a Saturday afternoon, you will find after one o'clock that the freight office is locked up and the agents and clerks are having a holiday while you may be desirous of shipping stock; it may be as is the custom- so it will be on the market early the following week. The fixation of the hours of labour and wages is only one of the difficulties with which we are confronted, difficulties that are having a depressing influence on agriculture. How can our farmers compete with other countries when they are so handicapped? And yet they have to compete against the surplus of the world in the home market. We hear the Minister of Labour (Mr. Murdock) and others say, "Oh, we must keep up the rate of wages to the high standard at which it has been for a long time." Yet we are expected to compete with other countries where the scale of wages is very low indeed. This naturally necessitates our having some protection against outside competition, and it is the absence of adequate protection under which our manufacturers are labouring at the present time.
But this handicap is not confined to the manufacturers only. To my mind those engaged in agriculture are suffering just as much

on this account as any other class. Consequently when the Minister of Immigration (Mr. Robb) states that his government are endeavouring to induce immigrants to go on the land, let me point out that the government ought to do something to enable those people to continue on the land after they settle there. It is only a few days ago in connection with the dumping clause in the tariff that the minister pointed out that, about a year ago, owing to a surplus of butter in the New York market the price dropped very low, and they dumped thirty or forty carloads of that surplus on the Montreal market, with the result that the price immediately went up again in the United States. But did he point out the effect that had on the market in this Dominion? No, he stopped there. To make the story complete, he should have pointed out the depressing influence the export of that surplus from a country with a high protective tariff had on the Canadian market. In order that the price in the United States should be maintained it was disposed of in this country. That is a fair example of a practice which is doing more to injure this Dominion to-day than anything else that can be mentioned. The United States is a highly protected country. They endeavour to maintain and so regulate their markets as to afford a profitable price; if they have a surplus of any kind they get rid of it somewhere, and apparently the easiest way to get rid of it is to ship it to Canada. They are continually doing that; it has been going on for years. Let me give some figures with regard to our imports of some commodities grown on the farm during the years 1920 to 1924 inclusive. In pork products alone during those years we imported 293,292,716 pounds, largely from the United States.

The hon. member desires that there shall be work for all, not only on the farms, but in the towns. Is it not a fact that the pork to which he refers was imported to give work to the bacon factories, and that the bacon manufactured from it was exported?

Not at all. Of
these pork products 48,832,000 pounds was lard, and that could hardly have been imported for manufacture and subsequent export. But since the grading of hogs has come into effect in this country there is apparently no lard in a Canadian hog, so they have to bring it in from the United; States, and the tariff is so low that that is the source of supply at the present time. But we are also at the same time large exporters of pork products; we exported 666,769,000 pounds, which shows that we are in a position not only to produce enough for home consumption, but to export a large quantity in addition. That being so why not give the Canadian market to the Canadian farmer. The minister two or three years ago went over to Australia to negotiate a treaty with that country, and as a result of his efforts, and the efforts, I presume, of those who succeeded him, a treaty was arranged a year ago. Was any attempt made to safeguard in that treaty the interests of those engaged in agriculture? On the contrary, on fourteen out of sixteen different points, agriculture suffered. It is true the treaty has not been presented to parliament, but the treaty was made and signed and announced by the government of Australia subject to ratification by the parliament of Canada. We exported 71,000,000 pounds of butter during that five-year period and we imported 15,000,000 pounds. I suppose in the main to relieve some protected country the consignment the minister referred to came in in that way; the great bulk of the butter which is imported into this country comes in under those conditions. The same is true
with regard to eggs; and by the way, under the Australian treaty the tariff on eggs is reduced to one cent per dozen.

I would not be surprised at my hon. friend objecting to the pork industry being referred to, but when it comes to eggs, surely he should not object.

They are closely associated
with ham.

Ou^imports of eggs were 35,788,000 dozen and our exports were 23,453.955 dozen. You can understand the demoralizing effect of a surplus of eggs and apples coming into this country from the United States, you can understand what the dumping of these commodities into Canada at certain periods of the year means to our people. Our seasons are from two to six weeks later than in the United States, and we have long, severe winters here which entail excessive cost in the production of butter and cheese as compared with the cost of production in countries like Australia and New Zealand where the cattle run out the year around. But the government say, "Our policy is to reduce the cost of living; we must keep the price of everything down below what it is in some other countries and our working people will get the benefit." This is the encouragement which the minister is offering to agriculturists to come to this country, the inducement he is offering to those who are on the land to stay there. Keep down the cost of living; keep wages up at the peak; put as many in the civil service as you can, establish a short day, ensure them a livelihood, and provide and old age pension for everybody who will not work. I have said this
before. I have criticized not only this government but previous governments for their shortcomings in many respects.
I recall that.

But we were never
in such desperate straits as we are to-day having to meet a burden in connection with our national debt which is increasing at the rate of something like $100,000,000 per year. There is only one place for us to end up if this continues. If it was a private individual he would be in the hands of the sheriff; but I do not know who would make foreclosure in the case of a government that is pursuing such a reckless policy as this one is. We cannot go on as we are going-that is absolutely certain. It may be that we will require a Mussolini, or some dictator, to take control of matters and put them on a business basis; but just as sure as the sun rises in the morning, this policy cannot continue* without absolute ruin overtaking us. attempt being made by the government to meet this condition and to curtail expenses. On the contrary there is a most lavish expenditure going on in the various departments of the government which should not be allowed.

When the hon. member
who has just resumed his seat was speaking, I could not help thinking of an old saying that "so long as a boiler can blow off steam it is safe". But a boiler blowing off steam never does any good; it just makes a noise and nobody pays any heed to it. The hon. member for East Calgary (Mr. Irvine) made a remark -I do not know that it is worth taking notice of considering the personality of the gentleman who uttered it-that I was rather lazy in doing my work in the House. I think there is not another hon. member in this House, outside of that hon. gentleman, who would have so little regard for himself as to make a statement of that kind. I have been a member for four years and during those four sessions there have only been five occasions when I have not been in my seat either in the afternoon or in the evening, when the House was opened. I think that is at least an indication that I am attending to my duties and looking after the interests of the people who sent me here.
A great deal has been said about people leaving Canada, 'but I do not intend to take up much of the time of the House in dealing with this matter. When I pick up a newspaper and read such things and then listen to what is said here, it sets me thinking. The other day I came across a copy of the Vernon News. It has been a Tory paper ever since it was started, and therefore I think we can rely upon what it says. A certain man who had spent six months in California, upon returning to Canada made this statement:
The lure of the south should be forgotten for it is largely a myth.
He stated that while it is true that wages are fairly high in the country to the south, it is equally true that the cost of living is high also. Many workmen are out of employment, indeed many are in destitute circumstances; and then he advises people who are inclined to go to the south to think seriously before taking that step, and he winds up by saying "Canada is far ahead of California". I turn to another paper and I read that "in Philadelphia last year there were 155 murders and 176 people committed suicide. Is that an indication of prosperity in the States?

It would suggest that the undertakers were prosperous!
(Mr. Sutherland.]

That may be. Then I turn
to what President Coolidge says. He states that there is eight times as much crime in the United States to-day as there is in Great Britain. And yet we hear a lot about the numbei; of people who are out of employment in the Mother Country. Surely we should pay some attention to what the press of the United States says. Then I turn to another paper- a good Conservative paper too-and it speaks of two1 spinning mills being started in Vancouver that are going to employ 150 people. I read in the same paper that in the month of May in Vancouver there were 670 permits taken out to build houses at a valuation of $2,929,385. Does that look as if this country is going to ruin? If it does why should they build these houses.
It is the same in Montreal.

Then I read in the Financial Times that this country is entering upon a wave of prosperity that it has not experienced for years, and I think that that statement is correct. Bearing these facts in mind why should the time of this House be taken up day after day, and week after week, in trying to hold Canada up to ridicule, and to condemn the members of the government and the country for political reasons. That is why this propaganda is being carried on and for no other purposes. Is that why we are sent down here and paid salaries for? Is that what the people of Canada want us to consume the time of the House with? If it is, I do not want to come back.
You had better speak for yourself.	.
I should like to have a statement from the minister regarding the colonization associations which are getting or likely to get grants this year.
There is a grant to the Salvation Army of $25,000, and to the Scottish Emigration Aid Society of $5,000, and under the heading " unforeseen " an amount of $5,000 making a total of $35,000.

these immigrants on their arrival in the country to endeavour to direct them in the right way towards getting on the land either in the western prairie provinces, in northern Ontario-for example-or in Quebec, or in the Maritime provinces? What efforts are being made by the department to look after them after their arrival in this country?

There is pretty complete
direction work carried on now from all parts of Canada, not only by the officers of the department, but outside of them. There are throughout this country interested people in different communities who do everything they can to help the newcomer to get settled. Yes, they help very materially.

I think one of the troubles has been, not only at the present time but in the past-and I am not particularly offering any criticism of this government in regard ot it, but of all governments-that there has been too much tendency when immigrants came to this country to give them no attention after they got here, but simply to let them look out for themselves, so to speak. I think that in the future we should all, whatever government is in power, make a greater endeavour than in the past to give proper attention to people who are coming here, from foreign lands particularly, but even to people coming from the British Isles. These people are coming to a new country, and1 it is difficult for them to acclimatize themselves, if they ore absolutely neglected by the government. I remember well a letter written some years ago by a good Liberal friend of the present government, Mr. John King-
I know him very well.

The minister remembers
him. He is a very estimable gentleman.
Indeed he is.

He wrote a letter to the
Quebec Telegraph in which he suggested a method of looking after the immigrants after their arrival along the lines of lending them small amounts of money to be paid back gradually. After they had cleared a certain number of acres of land they were to be loaned a small amount, and after they had Cleared a further quantity of land they were to be loaned a further amount. I do not remember the details but the principle was that some assistance was to be given them by the government of the day to look after them after their arrival in this country. I am not advocating the details of the scheme
11 p.m. as proposed by him-in fact I do not remember them well enough-but I believe the principle is right, that we should give greater attention to these people and not depend so much as we have 2674
in the past upon voluntary organizations to look after strangers coming to our shores. Indeed, I think it is altogether likely that if in the past we had given more attention to the people on their arrival in Canada we would have held more than we have been able to hold. I think the government should give serious consideration to the question of having their immigrants looked after in that regard, and possibly also in the way advocated by Mr. John King in this country. The minister is familiar with his proposition as he is nodding his head.

I am glad my hon. friend
approves of that idea, because the department now is taking every care to welcome the settler, and as far as possible to follow him up and see that he is properly settled. With reference to the policy advocated by Mr. John King of loaning money, and so forth is concerned, I am not prepared to endorse that.

I do not believe there is enough effort made-and I have mentioned this in the House before-to settle the bush lands of this country. We have an immense country practically uninhabited between North Bay and the Manitoba boundary. We have a territory 700 miles in length and wide enough to make an area of 300,000 square miles; in fact, large enough to make an area equal to the German Empire and the British Isles combined which have over a hundred million people between them and yet in northern Ontario we have but a population of 150,000. We have some of the finest agricultural land in the world in that district. There are those sections which have been settled, where the people have cut their homes out of the bush, and they have as fine farms as you will find in any section of Ontario or Quebec. I believe the government should do more to encourage immigration to these districts. It has been the policy not only of the government, because they handle the lands in the prairie provinces, but it has been the policy of the different railways, to encourage immigration rather to the prairie provinces, for the reason, from the railway standpoint, that they get a longer haul. It gives them more freight to carry. But for the purpose of bringing freight to the railway, for the purpose of filling in that gap where there is not sufficient traffic for the railway. I think a greater effort should be made by this government, or any other government handling the immigration affairs of the country, to get a type of immigration, as there is a type of immigrant in Europe, anxious to come to bush lands and clear their

Where will we get that type of man?

We have I believe in Europe certain classes who wish to come to that class of land. For example I am told that some of the northern European people, the Finlanders, are people who wish to go on bush lands and cut their homes out of bush lands. We have many Finlanders in my section of the country who make very excellent settlers, providing they are not that extreme kind of Finlander who are a little inclined to be socialistically red and carry it to the extent of red socialism. Of course since my hon. friend asks that question, we have right here in Canada-I am not speaking of immigration in this case-a class of people who prefer bush lands to any other, coming from the province to which my hon. friend belongs, the good odd province of Quebec. When they leave their own province of Quebec they prefer to go to a section where there is bush land rather than to go to ;a prairie section. That is my understanding .and I think I am correct in that. There are [DOT]other classes of European people who prefer bush lands though I cannot name them. I have read of them. Perhaps it is the Norwegians.
The Poles?

I cannot answer that, I do not know, but there are some other people in Europe who prefer bush lands, and we should make a greater effort to get more of the people to settle on those lands, especially in Ontario and Quebec and the eastern provinces, rather than to get people to settle in the prairie provinces.
What is the process followed once an immigrant is landed on Canadian shores?

What type of immigrant does the hon. member refer to-the agriculturist? Generally speaking, the effort has been along the lines advocated by the hon. member for Fort William and Rainy River as far as possible, to have them go to the east, in the belief that they will drift westwards. Perhaps the boys will go west. But, when they start out with the idea in their minds that they want to go to Alberta, you cannot make them remain in the east.
Does the department assure them that they will have work?

We do not allow them to
come unless we have an assurance that there is going to be work for them.
Does the minister say that fifty per cent of the farm labourers who came to Canada had jobs provided for them before they came?

I think there was an understanding that they would get work. I think we had an understanding with the transportation companies who asked for permits for certain numbers. If we had a guarantee that they would get work we gave them permits. Sometimes the companies and sometimes individuals asked for these immigrants. Sometimes we are found fault with for following up and refusing permits, but we discovered that there had been a system of trafficking in permits, and that is why we are careful to follow them up and see that there is no trafficking in the permits, and that the permits are genuine.

I am glad the minister has not committed himself further than saying, "I think so"; because I have a distinct recollection of many incidents that have come to my attention of immigrants who have come in during recent years who have not been provided with jobs and who were unable to get them.
We do not . guarantee jobs.

Is that, true or not?

Surely we are entitled to know how the money is to be spent.

The only grants we are making are $25,000 to the Salvation Army, $5,000 to the Scottish Immigration Aid Society, and $5,000 for unforeseen expenses, or a total of $35,000. If my hon. friend is referring to vote No. 63 the figure he has given is wrong; the amount is $1,210,000.

The minister a moment ago said that if I had looked up the British Hansard I should have found that Colonel Amery, in the statement which I quoted a short while ago, was referring to the British Empire settlement scheme. That may be true, but the fact is that the statement,
bald as it is, was scattered throughout the British Isles and undoubtedly misled hundreds of prospective emigrants. I hold in my hand another document, a letter published by the Canadian Chamber of Commerce in London, the deliberate purpose of which was to offset the misleading and "vindictive effort", as it is put, to discourage British immigration to Canada. I will quote a part of this letter.
Recognising the fact that her duty towards the settler does not terminate when he lands on her shores, the Dominion government has made the most careful and complete arrangements for giving new arrivals something much more than a chance to succeed in their new surroundings.
What are these wonderful opportunities?
The men are given the opportunity for training under competent supervision.
Where are these training schools and where is the competent supervision? They are-
Safe-guarded in regard to the purchase of farms and stock, loans are being advanced under the most advantageous terms, and yet something that looks exceedingly like an organized campaign is being waged at the present time against emigration to the Dominion.
These hostile letters and articles almost invariably refer to conditions in the urban centres. That there is unemployment in Canadian cities and towns is admitted, and is a regrettable fact. It is one that has to be faced every winter, just as it has to be in every town and city in the British Islands, but the Canadian government has never encouraged emigration to its centres of population. Its whole effort has been to secure men and women for the land and to keep them from the congested centres. It is nowhere contended that there is unemployment on the farms, and any man willing and physically able to work can obtain employment there.
I may tell the minister that the whole statement is grossly misleading. The last part of it is partly true, and only dangerously so. We can provide employment for a large number of men on the farms in western Canada, but only during a short season, and the rest of the time they must shift for themselves. I have still another document, some of the immigration propaganda of this government. I am informed that it is distributed at the Wembley exhibition, dn red and black letters the title appears, "Canada the New Homeland''; and on the very first page there is the following sentence, indicative of the psychology of the men who write this sort of stuff:
Canada is situated mainly in the north temperate zone, in the latitudes in which the people of the United Kingdom have been born and brought up.
This is absolutely true, every word of it; but it does not give the unfortunate man who reads it any conception of our climatic conditions. It does not say that we are in the same latitude as a part of Siberia. Now, the weather here has not hurt any of us; certainly it is not hurting me, for I rather enjoy it.

It is a land of homes-the "New Homeland" of the British people-a land where all who are intelligent and industrious may reasonably expect success.

Do hon.

They are not any worse off than the farmers' in any other part of the world.

That is not the point. The point is that these statements are a deliberate misrepresentation on the part of this government of the conditions that exist. And I could go further and quote other statements. These statements are made in government propaganda in spite of what is said by the agents of this government itself. I hold in my hand the report of Dr. Tory on agricultural credit, which is worth reading by any hon. member. He cites there exactly what I have believed and stated in this House for many years. This is what he says:
Much is being said to-day about keeping young men on the farm, retaining them on the land in our own country. The truth is that except for the men of the hardy pioneering type, who are able and willing to venture on the virgin soil of the northern areas in Canada, it is almost impossible for men of limited means to get established as farmers.
That is the government's own agent speaking.
A certain number of course inherit from their fathers, but for the great majority of the young men of this generation it costs more to get established as farmers, in both money and energy, in any of the older settled parts of Canada than to enter upon either industrial or professional careers. Without question eastern Canada to-day is losing some of her best rural human stock, sons and daughters of those who pioneered and made this country what it is, people who brought to the country those simple arts of life which helped them to establish their families and their small communities as social units, because they do not see how they can under present conditions establish themselves in a reasonable time in anything like reasonable comfort.
These are the sons and daughters of our Canadian farmers, not the unacclimatized, in-

experienced immigrant labouring under the greatest difficulties. He continues:
It can be stated without fear of successful contradiction that it is not all the lure of the city and the pleasures of town life that attract our young Canadians to the cities and towns. It is, at least in part, because the occupations offered seem to give a more immediate hope of reasonable prosperity.
It is very easy for those living in comparative affluence, like my hon. friend from Cariboo (Mr. McBride), to say that young men should do as their fathers did. The truth is their fathers had no alternative offered of the kind offered by the centres of industry to-day:
What has just been stated applies not only to eastern Canada but to western Canada as well. Land within easy reach of transportation must be paid for some way and it costs money and energy to secure it. To put the above aspect of the matter on no higher basis than that of personal advantage it is in the interest of every business organization, industrial establishment and financial corporation in this country, that a way should be found to offer young people of Canada such a reasonable chance of success in this country that they will desire to establish themselves as farmers.
There is what Dr. Tory says after an investigation made no later than last year. His statement directly and deliberately refutes the propaganda of this government, but the programme continues.
Will my hon. friend read that statement and the pamphlet again? I cannot follow his argument. It seems to me Dr. Tory simply says what the pamphlet says.
Of course, you cannot convince a man against his will, and I am not going to try. I have not the time, for I have a lot to say.
You always have.

I am not one of those who blame the government for the actual conditions that exist. I do not. I will tell the House in a few moments upon whom I b'ame the conditions that exist in western Canada, and it is not wholly upon the government sitting opposite; my hon. friends to my right must take a very considerable share of responsibility in the matter. Behind the fence to the back of the House, and running over a beautiful sweep of park land was a crop standing in the stook, and the stooks were so thick as to make one wonder how the artist could have got enough room to paint them all in. It was the sort of crop that one sees in this country once in perhaps ten or fifteen years. Off to one side was standing a splendidly built man in the

stage uniform of Jack Canuck. He had on the broad brimmed sombrero, and the English riding breeches, which are very rarely seen in western Canada. He was wearing an open shirt with the cowboy tie, and to everyone who looked at the picture he was uttering these words, "Monarch of all I survey." Not a word about the mortgage companies, not a word about the banks or his debts to them, not a word about taxes or anything else. The wonderful impression was thrown out upon the minds of all who were unfortunate enough to be receptive, that all they had to do was to come here and within a short space of time, almost as quick as the clicking of your fingers, they would appear like that wonderful gentleman and be the monarch of similar possessions.
That kind of propaganda is condemned by Mrs. Harrison Bell. It is condemned by myself. It is condemned, and must be condemned by every honest-minded man in this country who stands for the good of Canada.
This wonderful gentleman who was standing in the middle of this painting, may I ask if he was one of the egg inspectors of the Minister of Agriculture?

May I say, Mr. Chairman, if the government is really serious in this matter-I cannot believe they are-I think they are just talking for political purposes-but if they are really serious they would censor all the very recent publications of the department. They would censor the publication of this report by Doctor Tory, which makes statements both this year and last which exceed the most extravagant statements ever made by any hon. member on this side of the House. In the opening paragraphs of his report last year, he compares current conditions on the farms of Canada with those existing in Germany in 1875-the most desperate conditions that ever existed in agriculture in Germany, when homes were burned, when much was destroyed, and the countryside was destitute. It is like reading a commentary on conditions here. Doctor Tory's report this year is almost as striking as it was last year.
Then we have the report of the National Conference regarding winter employment in Canada, printed at Ottawa, by F. A. Acland, Printer to the King's Most Excellent Majesty It is not my purpose to quote at length from this report, because that has already been done by my hon. friend from Centre Winnipeg (Mr. Woodsworth) and myself in the debate on unemployment and immigration. I say that this report should also be censored if the gov-
[Mr. E. J. Garland.1
ernment is not prepared to face the actual facts and conditions rather than covering them up with statements of the kind I have quoted from "Canada, the New Homeland."
The other day, Mr. Chairman, I had the unfortunate experience of meeting three fine, moderately young Scotchman out of employment. They were three of the poor chaps who had come up here from Cape Breton. Let me tell this House their story.
These three men had come to Canada as a result of the propaganda carried on in Scotland by the British Empire Steel Corporation. They had seen advertisements in the Glasgow Herald, and in local papers, urging experienced miners to come to the Cape Breton coal fields, where they would be assured of a job at from five to six dollars a day, with steady work. These three men came here on the strength of that statement. Two of them happened to be married, one had, I think, seven children, and the other ten. The third man was unmarried. After they had been here some time they were encouraged by the company to bring out their families.
Ten years of age and drawing six dollars a day?
What is the man talking about, Mr. Chairman?

I wanted to ask the hon. member a question. He said that he had met three young Scotchmen who had come to this country, and who were promised six dollars a day for working in the mines. I am asking the age of these young men. I understood the hon. member to say they were ten years of age.
There is really no use in making any comment on that question. I say that one of these married men had seven children, another ten, and the third man was unmarried.
Was he a Scotchman?

Yes. The
two married men were deliberately encouraged by the company to bring their families out here. The men naturally were glad to accept the encouragement, as all men feel rather lonely and gloomy at times when separated from their families. They took advantage of the company's offer to advance them the money required to pay the passage of their families. These two men brought their families out, and undertook that liability to the company. One of them, the father of the seven children, has not yet succeeded in paying off that liability. He has not had enough

Supply-Immigration
work in the two years to enable him to pay *off that debt. The other man had two grown sons who went and worked in the mines with him and who subjected themselves to the reduction of $5 from each pay cheque until they were finally able to pay off their debt to the company amounting to over $600. That debt for transportation has only just been paid off after two years, with three members of the family working in the mines.
The strike came on. They endured conditions just as long as they could, and finally decided it was no use staying in that area, and they left it to find work. The reason why they left it they told very graphically. They had gone up to Sydney, and there they saw an advertisement stating that 800 men and women were wanted in the ibeet fields of Alberta. On that very day they arrived here in Ottawa, the hon. member for East Calgary (Mr. Irvine) rose in this House and read a telegram from one of the representatives of labour in Calgary to the effect that there was no further employment in the beet fields, that this order was filled long ago. Whatever truth there is in that I am not concerned with now. But it was on the strength of that advertisement that these men started west. How they were going to get west they did not know. They were going to try and get a job on the way perhaps. They went from Moncton to Quebec, and on to Montreal, beating their way, with no money in their pockets. Their experiences on this trip were heartrending to anyone who heard them-suspected by everybody, driven around from one place to another, driven from doorways. Let me give you one illustration.
These men had stopped in the shelter of a railway embankment to cook a billy-can of tea. Dusk was falling, and just as soon as they were ready to partake of their tea, along came one of the railway policemen and ordered them off, using abusive language. They ran up the embankment, and as they ran the policeman struck one of them with his baton three times on the back. When they reached the top of the embankment the policeman fired two shots after them with his revolver. That is the sort of treatment they got-these men who were looking for work.
Here is another experience they had. Going into one of the towns along the way, they noticed the ties were on fire, caused by cinders dropped from the engine. They put the fire out, and approaching the town they met a policeman, and told him what they had done. He said to them in language which I cannot repeat in this House "What is the company to you? Do you think I am going to believe a story of that kind? Do you mean to say you expect me to believe you went and put out that fire? What interest have you got in the company?"
Did the hon. member hear the other side of the story?
I have heard the stories of the three men and each one was corroborated by the other.

the other side?

I am telling you the story as I heard it. Hon members can put what interpretation they like on it. These are the facts as I have heard them recited by these men. By the way, they spent one weekend in Montreal trying to find a job; they went everywhere, along the docks, the wharves, and elsewhere. There was no work for them. They told us here that there were many unemployed in that city. They came to Ottawa. The first thing they did here was to apply to the employment agency. And these people are not the feeble-minded or the old; they are the healthy, the young, the best blood and brain of this Dominion, who have been born, raised and educated at enormous expense to Canada.
How long will this exodus to the United States continue; how long can this country stand the drain of 200,000 or 300,000 per year of its best young people? Why are those young men and women leaving Canada?
The Ottawa Citizen in another editorial not very long ago said this:
The situation for Canada is far more serious than merely that the young men are "leaving their priceless heritage to the keeping of the older generation". They are leaving Canada entirely, to become citizens of another country. Many thousands of the Canadian men who came back from overseas inspired with a greater love for the homeland, and a zeal to serve Canada in peace as in war, have been driven abroad by the pressure of economic circumstances. They found barriers to opportunity raised against them. Entrenched interests have established themselves as toll-gate keepers who take higher toll than young men are prepared to pay for the privilege of living in this country.
I could go on quoting from many sources as to the conditions that exist.
Quote your own case.

I am not so puffed up with myself as to imagine that my own case is due to any ability on my part. The fact that I have the distinction of being in this House to speak for these people has only been possible because of the contemptible conditions under which many of my own unfortunate people have had to live in recent years. I have been sent down here by them because those conditions were wrong, so that I might tell the House about them and try and get a remedy. I have in my hand a few other dispatches. Here is one dated April 2, 1925, and reads:
To give one an idea of the extent of the exodus of settlers from the south country, it might be mentioned that on last Friday's train there were seven carloads of settlers' effects, and on Monday's train there were eighteen. It is stated that -there will be eight or ten more carloads on .to-marro-w's train.
I was down here when this happened, but when I read this item from a local correspondent I was shocked. Then I found in the Ottawa Journal on the same day the following:
Large party of immigrants on way to Canada.
Thirty families leave Liverpool under overseas settlement plan to work farms in Dominion.
On the one hand you will find people who have struggled to make a living gcing out by the trainload, and people being brought in by the boat load. They will not stay until economic condi:ions are improved in this country, until rapid and progressive steps are taken by the administration to see to it that the question of unemployment is solved, and the condition of agriculture is solved, and ;hey can do it if they will turn their attention to it with a will, which I would like to see them do.

Having listened to this hardy
annual from my hon. friend, I dc not wish to delay my own estimates by making another speech. I am not going to quote any of the figures of the movement of immigration. I will not tire the House by reading the whole of their letter. This letter in part reads:
In our report we have made certain recommendations with a view to improving the system under which the children migrate to Canada and, in particular, have recommended that no children under school-leaving age should be assisted to proceed to Canada-a recommendation which has been adopted by the Secretary of State for the Colonies and by the Dominion government. At the same time we found that, generally speaking, the existing arrangements were satisfactory, that the children were regularly inspected and well looked after by the societies responsible for bringing them to Canada, and that the prospects for the boys and girls in Canada are better than they would have been had they remained in the United Kingdom.
Here is another clause in the letter:
The selection of the children is, and always has been, vested entirely in the hands of the Dominion government. It is not to be expected that there should not be a number of failures among these children, but the vast majority have undoubtedly become good Canadian citizens.
My hon. friend who speaks annually on the immigration problem is himself an immigrant. On his own statement he came to this country not as well off as he is to-day. It seems to me his presence in this parliament, the clothes that he wears and the company with whom he associates are evidence that he is not doing too badly in Canada. He comes from Alberta and apparently he has done very well. I want to say that the gentlemen surrounding me and the gentlemen sitting opposite me are in a position to speak for the province of Ontario and the province of Quebec. My hon. friend has found fault with the literature sent out and published by the federal government, and if I understand it he claims that we misrepresented the climate, and that we have not told people of the rigorous climate of Canada, that we have submitted a picture of bams and houses that is altogether misleading. The climate of Alberta is of very attractive quality, and this quality has a very important bearing on the possibilities of development northward and on industrial and more particularly agricultural activities. however, by reason of contiguity to the coast province has a rather moderate climate.

Alberta has a greater diversity of surface than the other prairie provinces. The new province gave promise of becoming one of the brightest, jewels in the crown of empire. Richly endowed by nature with broad and fertile agricultural lands, a wealth of mineral resources, and surpassing beauty of mountain scenery.

does the government of Alberta speak for the province, or does the hon. member for Bow River?

I desire briefly to
refer to one particular aspect of this immigration question, namely, that with regard to child immigration. A year ago this question was discussed in the House and there is no reason why I should now go over the ground then covered. However, since that time the subject has been discussed rather fully following a visit from Miss Margaret Bondfield and investigations by the social workers of this country. These investigations throw some light upon this very important question. As I said last year we ought to look at this matter both from the standpoint of the immigrant child and from that of the welfare of this country. We have recorded a very large number of instances where children have been mistreated in Canada and this would seem to show that the supervision is not as good as it should foe. On the other hand, we have had so many instances of children being brought into Canada who were not suited for immigration that it would indicate that the selection has not been either careful or wise. As I pointed out last year, we are extremely careful about the character of our grain; we try to get the best seed possible. And we are equally careful in the matter of live stock. But we pay much less attention to the character of the girls and boys, the human stock, whom we are importing from the Old Land. I shall quote briefly from a report which has been sent me by the Social Service Council of Canada, an organization on which are represented a large number of churches and social agencies in this country, and which I heard quoted the other day as an authority by the hon. member for Lotbiniere (Mr. Vien):
Previous to the visit of Miss Margaret Bondfield, M.P. and a delegation of the overseas settlement committee to Toronto, a further effort was made to ascertain the effect upon Toronto of juvenile immigration. By co-operation of local social service agencies specially interested in child life, an investigation was made by trained workers as to the number of persons in Toronto who came to Canada as child immigrants. Two hundred cases were recorded, twenty-four of whom were included in the records already quoted from the Toronto General Hospital.
The minister a little while ago said that certain members on his side were able to speak for the old province of Ontario. Now, I am quoting here figures taken from statistics collected by social workers in Ontario, which province has received a larger proportion of juvenile immigrants than any other section of Canada. At page 41 of this report there appears a statement with regard to these two hundred cases:

The pamphlet then goes to analyze these figures:
What is the significance of these figures? Certainly not, that all juvenile immigrants are immoral, or defective or dependent. These two hundred cases were collected through agencies or persons chiefly concerned with relief or correction or some other aspect of social service. The two hundred represent, therefore, the percentage of the failure of the system through which they were recruited for Canada, rather than its normal product. The reports of the Superintendent of Juvenile Immigration for Canada and the publications of tho immigrating homes and agencies, as well as earlier sections of this report, have told the other side of the story. Most of us know desirable citizens of Canada who reached these shores as child immigrants. Nor do we consider that statistics on this subject, collected in Toronto, are likely to be characteristic of conditions in cities in other parts of Canada. As many more than two-thirds (74 per cent in 1923 Year Book) of the juvenile immigrants to Canada settle in Ontario, it is altogether likely that Toronto has more than her fair proportion of the failures among her dependent citizens Granting these considerations, your committee is still of the opinion that conditions prevailing in Toronto justify them in thinking that the' success or failure of juvenile immigration should not be judged only by the records of the juvenile immigrants while wards of the immigrating agency. The statistics quoted above show the "dangerous ages" to be just the years when these wards, for the first time, become independent of the home.
They are supported by the evidence of the social workers who visited places in the province where these boys and girls have been placed on farms or in country homes. Again and again they report employers and neighbours as remarking on the foolish use made by these young people of their accumulated wages and their new-found liberty. Many seem to use their freedom to leave the country and taste the pleasures and temptations of the city. In this way the system of juvenile immigration vitally affects city life; and yet, neither the city nor the province, except in Manitoba, has any say in the placement of immigrant children within their borders.
Reference is here made to the province of Manitoba. I may say that the social workers interested in the placement of children in that province have stated to me that they are very much afraid of the incoming of such large numbers of immigrant children, and that in fact some of the immigration agencies have tried to act quite independently of the pro-

vincial authorities in placing these children. This is a very serious state of affairs.
I shall quote a few very brief sentences from the conclusions and recommendations of the Social Service Council of Canada. It seems to me these are very reasonable and should be carefully considered by the government, especially as they are given to the public after the visit of Miss Bondfield and after a great deal of discussion had had taken place about these agencies:
The inspection as now carried out by the federal government and the immigrating agencies is often perfunctory and inadequate. One agency has but one inspector, a man of eighty years of age. More generally, the visits of the inspectors are few and ill-managed, and the inspectors are not always suited to their work.
Again:
The apprentice contract should be standardized for different sexes, ages and types, and be convincingly just for both employer and employee.
Again:
That no immigrant child, even if otherwise satisfactory. should be accepted by the Dominion immigration officials in Britain who has not been subjected to three tests-tuberculin test, Wasserman reaction test, and a psychiatric test.
Again:
That while it is impossible to lay down rigid rules as to the desirable frequency of inspection. (a) No child should be sent to a foster home from an agency until that foster home has been inspected and passed upon by an official duly appointed by the provincial authorities or by the Department of Immigration.
And once again:
That as the demand in Canada is for children to work on farms or in households, only boys and girls of post-school age should be brought to Canada by immigrating agencies.
That last recommendation is, I think, one that was given by Miss Bondfield to the imperial authorities. At this late hour, Mr. Chairman, I do not wish to enlarge upon these recommendations, but I do feel that I ought not to allow this opportunity to pass without very definitely placing these facts and suggestions before the committee and urging that they be given serious consideration by the department. I fancy that we ought to look forward to the years to come when the boys and girls from our own homes will be sufficient to gradually spread our population across the Dominion. I hope that the time will come when, for the sake of Canada, we shall not be forced to bring in young girls and boys to work in our homes and on our farms. In the interests of the immigrant children, although in many respects life in Canada may be superior to life in the slums of Great Britain, I urge that we must have a much better system of inspection than we have had in the past.

Mr. Chairman, in answer to
my hon. friend from' Centre Winnipeg (Mr. Woodsworth) I think I placed on record a moment ago the statement of the Hon. Margaret Bondfidd, who visited Canada purposely to look into this question of child immigration. Her report showed that the children had done fairly well in this country, and that, generally speaking, they were well cared for. I am not going into the details of the report issued by the social service workers. One does not like to contradict welfare workers who are animated, no doubt, by a desire to help, but it seems to me that at least before broadcasting such a report they might have consulted the department and received more accurate information. To give my hon. friend an instance of only one inaccuracy, on page four of the report the statement is made, that in the last fifteen years Canada has brought seventy-five thousand juveniles to her shores, and the movement is said to be steadily increasing in volume. The total influx of juvenile children, not including children belonging to parents, for the fifteen years ending March 31, 1924, is not 75,000, but 21,552. The total number of juvenile immigrants brought to Canada since 1868 is just about 80,000. The total of the arrivals for the ten years ending March 31, 1924, is under 10,000, and the total for the previous ten years was almost about 25,000. To get the highest number for any one year, we have to go back to 1905-1906, when 3,264 juvenile immigrants came in, the only time in the history of the movement when it exceeded 3,000 a year.

Might I ask the
minister to comment on the particular statistics which I gave? Does he question those?

I have not looked into them
at all, but if they are no more correct than the one I have noticed, I should not like to waste a busy man's time looking into them.

Mr. Chairman, there is just one aspect of the child immigration problem that I think this committee might well take into consideration. In Canada, indeed in Ottawa itself, we have a tremendous number of orphan children-our own Canadian children, born of our own Canadian people-anxious for a home. Ladies who have gone down to visit these places have told me that the children will climb on their knees and hug them, so anxious are they for some affection. Now, it occurs to me that while these orphans all over Canada are left dependent largely upon voluntary charity, it is not a very good policy to be

spending taxes on the importation of children from other countries. That is my comment. I think our duty is to our own children first. Instead of looking after them as we should, we leave them largely dependent upon what chance contributions gentle souls throughout the country may be in a position to make.

Does not
my hon. friend know that the care of these children in his province is under the direction
of the government he supports, led by Premier 'Greenfield and-not this government?

Yes; and
I also know that even in that province we are put to our wits' ends to provide homes for mental defectives, the direct result of the importation of these child immigrants. Now, Mr. Chairman, the minister had a lot of fun out of the few remarks he made after I had finished. I would disabuse his mind of one or two misapprehensions. I agree with him heartily that the propaganda published by the Alberta Department of Agriculture over the name of Mr. Hoadley does no more represent average conditions in Alberta than does his own propaganada.

Will my
hon. friend permit another question? Could he tell this committee if there is any government in this Dominion or anywhere else that he, with his Irish tendency to be " agin " the government would ever support?

No, Mr. Chairman. That is the kind of comment I would expect from the hon. gentleman, and it is all I would expect from him. The minister in his argument attempted to make it look as though Mr. Hoadley was speaking for the province of Alberta, and that of course the member for Bow River, although he was quite willing to let him speak for a portion, could not possibly be speaking for the whole of Alberta.

What about the records of
the whole cabinet?

Just a
moment, now. I have in my hand, as it so happens, two of the resolutions passed by the annual convention of the United Farmers of Alberta, which is the strongest farmers' organization in Canada, and is going to be stronger as a result of this government's action.

Do not be too sure of
that.

The hon.
member for Mackenzie (Mr. Campbell) corrects me; he says; "inaction." Inaction is correct. Now, let me paint this picture very clearly for the committee. Therefore, be it resolved, that the government be urged to discontinue their present expensive immigration policy and direct their efforts more towards bettering conditions so that the people we already have will wish to stay.
I take my mandate from that convention and not from Mr. Hoadley.

No, he had nothing to do with it.
