Mr. GAR,LAND (Bow River): Now, with regard to child immigration, again let me say, with all due respect to the remarks of the Minister of Immigration, that I am not altogether satisfied either with the inspection or with the general policy. I hold in my hand a despatch from Toronto dated May 18 of this year. It reads as follows:
Following the inquest here to-day the inquiry into the death of 18-year old Benjamin Berman, whose body was found in Toronto Bay last Thursday, Chief Coroner Graham referred to the apparent sub-normal mental condition of the boy's family, and declared that it was "a sad commentary on this Canada of ours that we have an immigration department that will permit the introduction into Canada of such a type as we have seen before us this afternoon."
I have another, but I do not want to quote it at length, regarding the suicide of some

unfortunate child immigrant, and the following quotation from the Vancouver Sun:
Sixteen-year-old boy came before the Toronto police ccurt this week on a charge of housebreaking. During the course of the trial it developed that the boy's father is an ex-convict and sub-normal in intellect.
One brother is now serving a term in the penitentiary and two others are deaf and dumb.
The five people are probably costing the Dominion of Canada $10,000 or more a year in loss through their depredations, cost of their trials and their keep.
And the sane, healthy people of the Dominion are paying the bill, incurred as it was through the fact that a mentally deficient father was permitted to come into this country.
There are difficulties, I admit, with regard to the checking or ascertaining of the mental condition of adult immigrants who come to Canada, but it is nothing as to the difficulty with regard to these orphan children, these child immigrants. The medical profession-* and I am quite sure the hon member for Fort William and Rainy River (Mr. Manion) will bear me out-will inform the House, if it is asked to, that you can examine the life history of any adult, checking up the life history also of father and grandfather, and make re-sonably sure whether there is any likelihood or any danger of insanity or of the development of any mental defect. Is that not true?
Oh, I think so.

In the case of these immigrant children, from the very nature of their origin one is justified in suspecting at least that there is mental taint. Where do they come from? Mostly from the orphan homes. In many cases you cannot even trace who their parents were; in many cases their parents are dead-died under extraordinary circumstances. I do not think the best interests of Canada are being served by enfiltrating the whole of our race with the dangerous types which undoubtedly will result from the importation of these child immigrants. The least we can ask is that before they are brought to these shores the strictest possible medical ecxamination be made Of every one of them individually. [DOT] The Minister of Immigration owes at least that much to Canada. I am personally opposed to child immigration. I am not opposed to adult immigration. I would permit any physically and mentally fit man or woman to come to Canada.
Mr. MACDONALD (Pictou) [DOT] Hear, hear.

Yes. But
I would not spend one dollar of the taxpayers' money to bring them here under the present conditions.

How did
you get here?

I got here
with my own money. I was not helped over on an assisted passage scheme. I did not have my farm financed. I did not have to take up an abandoned soldier settler's land at revalued prices. I came out here and took my chance at pioneering. Now, Mr. Chairman, may I ask that the minister take into serious consideration, more serious than he has indicated to-night, the remarks I have made? I have made them in all sincerity. My only interest is the welfare of Canada. Her welfare is mine. My children have been brought up here. We have also the statement of Miss Margaret Bondfield, who came here especially to look into the conditions, and who reported that these young people were being looked after very well here in Canada.
With reference to that regrettable incident in Toronto which my hon. friend referred to, the morning I read of it in the newspapers I wired to our agent in Toronto to make a report upon it, and I have that report here. I will admit at once that possibly in past years the medical inspection has been rather lax. There was a period in our history when we allowed people to come in here without a medical examination as strict as it is now, but the medical examination now is as strict as it possib!}' can be, and in addition to that, we have a very careful civil examination by our officers. In this particular case our records establish that the boy's father, a Russian Hebrew, arrived at Portland, Maine, on March 8, 1913, and was admitted destined to Toronto. In 1921 he returned to Poland on a visit, returning the same year. On May 23, 1923, 268j.
bis daughter, Gitla, aged seventeen, was admitted, and on September 8, 1923, his son, Benjamin, aged fifteen, was admitted. This is the boy whose death is being investigated. He was destined to the father at 138 Elizabeth street, Toronto, and according to our record passed medical inspection. On February 24, 1924, Mrs. Berman, aged forty-seven, together with her daughters, Ryfka and Nycha, aged twelve and nine years, respectively, were admitted, all destined to the husband and father at Toronto. Our record shows that each member of the family passed medical inspection at the port of entry.

Would the minister explain why it is necessary for Canada to spend millions of dollars annually to get immigrants, when the United States has millions offering without spending a cent? In fact, they are spending money to keep them out.

Canada is spending money to keep them out as well as the United States. We must control immigration. If my hon. friend is willing that we should wipe out all restrictions and allow the steamship companies to dump on our shores anyone they like, of course we would not need to spend the money.
Why should there be good immigration offering plentifully to the United States, but not to Canada?

The immigration must be
selected.
Mr. LeSUEUR: One of the questions which is important in immigration, and which I at least do not fully understand, is the extent and the details of co-operation between the federal and provincial immigration authorities; and secondly, after the immigrants have arrived here, what machinery have we got to follow them up and assist them, more or less to protect them in the early stages of their stay here?

Members using unparliamentary language are promptly called to order and generally satisfy the House with an explanation or an apology. If not they will be dealt with under rule 18 or punished as the House may think fit.
The tower is not ready for occupation yet.

Having quoted the expressions used by the right hon. gentleman, and I do not think he will deny having used them, I suggest that right hon. gentleman should apologize to the Chair, and if he refuses to do it, that he be dealt with according to our rules, and in any case that the remarks used by him should be deleted from Hansard.

I was not in when the hon. member started this interlude. I did not know that we' were revamping the proceedings of an hour or two ago. I came to see why the House was sitting so late. I do not know what the hon. member said when he began, but he referred to a remark I made in regard to a decision that was given by the hon. member for Labelle (Mr, Fortier) when he -was occupying the chair temporarily. A decision had been given, to which I took exception. An hon. member opposite remarked it was not debatable, to which I remarked, it was not speakable. Objection was taken, I presume, on the ground that comment cannot be offered on a decision of the Chair. That is right, and if an hon. member proceeds to speak of something that is not debatable, he can be called to order fMr. Cannon.1
and made to cease. But he cannot be made to withdraw unless he makes a remark attributing to another hon. member conduct unbecoming a gentleman. The word " unspeakable " is not such a word as has ever been ruled out of order in this House as attributing conduct unbecoming a gentleman.

In fairness to the right
hon. gentleman, before he came in I was quoting the expressions he had used, which were to the effect that the ruling given by the Chairman was a farce, secondly that it was a travesty, and thirdly that it was not speakable.

I consider, Mr. Chairman,
that this whole debate is out of order because according to rule 18 "the Speaker shall decide the point of order," which was the point of order referred to by the hon. member for Dorchester (Mr. Cannon) in regard to which certain remarks were made by the right hon. leader of the opposition. Rule 18 says:
The Speaker shall decide the point of order, which decision shall be subject to appeal to the House, but without debate. If there be no appeal, the decision of the Chair shall be final.
You, Sir, about an hour and a half ago gave your decision, and I consider it was final. Under the rule I have cited1 I do not think the hon. member had any right to open up this subject again.

We are not discussing the point, of order decided by the Chairman at that time. I am simply raising the point that the fight hon. leader of the opposition, contrary to his habit, has used veiy strong language, unparliamentary language, and I have no doubt that he will apologize as any hon. member who had done that should.
I have used no language which was unparliamentary at all and therefore cannot be made to withdraw.

I do not think the right
hon. gentleman can contend rightly that calling a decision of the Chair "a farce, a travesty and something unspeakable" is not unparliamentary.

I did not use the words
the hon. member has quoted. I used the word "unspeakable" or the words "not speakable" it is true. I said that a decision of that kind rendered the rules a farce. That language is not unparliamentary.

speechtext:
I am sorry that during my absence for a few moments, and while

the hon. member for Label I e (Mr. Fortier) Wats in the chair, this unfortunate incident occurred. I returned to the chamber to find that there was a dispute as to the words that were actually spoken.
By the hon. member for Lotbiniere (Mr. Vien).

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I understood the right
hon. leader of the opposition had used the expression, wdth respect to a decision the Chairman (Mr. Fortier) had given, that it was "unspeakable." I commented on the fact, and said I thought it was highly offensive for any such reflection to be oast on the Chair. Having given that ruling I do not feel called upon to repeat it at this late stage, but I do feel that the right hon. gentleman should withdraw the statement in fairness to the hon. member for Labelle.

The words that are unparliamentary have been reviewed in the rules over and over again and are to be found in Bourinot?	If it could be shown that the
word "unspeakable" or the words "not speak-able," which I used, can be regarded as unbecoming a gentleman, there would be some point to the objection raised.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I should like to deal
with this matter right now. Such a situation having developed, now is the proper time possibly to cite the authority which, apparently, deals with matters of this kind. In "Precedents of Proceedings in the House of Commons" volume 2, at page 234 under the title of "Speaker; his duties in keeping order in the House" I find the following:
It is impossible to lay down any specific rules upon this point or to declare beforehand what expressions are or are not contrary to order; so much depends upon the tone, and manner, and intention of the person speaking: something upon the person to whom they are addressed whether a minister in a responsible station, or a private member not in office;-whether the words are meant to be applied to his public conduct, or to his private character;-the degree of provocation which the member speaking had received from the person he alludes to:	All these considerations must be attended to at the moment, as they are infinitely various and cannot possibly be forseen in such a manner as that precise rules can be adopted with respect to them. When the Speaker observes upon any expression as personal and disorderly and tending to introduce heat and confusion, and this appears to be the general sense of the House, the member offending ought immediately to make an apology and to ask pardon of the House for this breach of their orders, in as large and liberal expressions as possible, so as in such apology to comprehend the person of whom the words were used.
It. is very difficult for me, not having been present, to interpret exactly the position that has developed out of this incident. It
occurred to me, however, that the expression used 'is one not ordinarily used, and if not out of order or if not unparliamentary, has nearly reached the point where it constitutes a reflection on the ruling that the hon. member for Labelle, as Chairman gave.

There was no reflection
on the ruling or the rules of the House, and one cannot be made to withdraw an expression unless it is unparliamentary. The very quotation which you, Mr. Chairman, have made shows that it was not. Nobody would suggest that it had reference to the private character or private conduct of the members, it referred- to a public act, and the quotation makes it very clear that I could not possibly be made to withdraw the expression.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I have not asked the
right hon. gentleman to withdraw his statement. I do say, however, that to my mind the expression he used approaches closely to a reflection upon the ruling of the Chair, and no hon. member has any right to reflect upon the ruling of the Chair.
I admit that.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
My right hon. friend,
in view of his long parliamentary experience should not have indulged in comment of such a nature wi h respect to a junior member who was temporarily occupying the Chair.

I admit that an hon.
member can be called to order for improperly commenting on a ruling of the Chair, but it is a very different thing to ask me to withdraw an expression which is neither ungentlemanly nor unparliamentary.

I am not asking the
hon. gentleman to do so.

Mr. Chairman will you
allow me-
Sit down.
Who said "sit down"?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I want this point of
order settled.

I certainly object to any
hon. gentleman telling me to sit down.
The remark was not nearly as objectionable as the one that was directed at me across the floor the other day.

I raiL.-d a point of order some time ago. I should like to know under what rule a question of order can be brought up an hour and a half after the decision has been given.

I should like to inform the hon. member that the question before the committee has been disposed of.
All right, if it has been disposed of.

I should like to ask if the government has seriously considered the advisability of coordinating the different immigration agencies as suggested by Sir Henry Thornton in his annual report on the Canadian National Railway; it seems to me that the suggestion was well worthy of consideration.

I did not read Sir Henry
Thornton's report. I did read his statement as reported in the public press which I imagine was the same thing. I should like to say that insofar as possible we are trying to cooperate with the two railways. We recognize that there is duplication particularly overseas, possibly in some places in the United States, but as far as possible we are trying to reduce expenditure and to adopt cooperative measures to the greatest possible extent.
The minister referred to Mr. Smith's retirement. Has his successor in London been appointed?
Mr. Little is now overseas.
How many private immigration agencies outside the Dominion are bringing in immigrants?

I could not tell my hon. friend that. There are many people who constitute themselves agents. There are many people who come to the department from time to time making representations that they are agents. We have no list of the number of such agencies.
I refer to such organizations as land companies, railway companies, and colonization associations.
And my hon. friend might add steamship companies, steamship agents and booking agents. We have no record of the number; they are world-wide in their activities.
To how many agencies do the government contribute in bringing immigrants into Canada?
I have already given that information three or four different times. My hon. friend will find it in Hansard.

Could the minister give us any idea as to the proportion of this vote which is spent for inspection work, that is looking

after the qualifications and characteristics of the immigrants who are applying for entrance, and the amount of money that is spent on attracting immigrants?
I can place on record a statement of the newspaper advertising and the lectures given if the hon. gentleman requires that.

I was not asking for anything very detailed, but I should like to have some information as to the respective cost of the inspection service on the one hand, and the lectures and advertising and so-called propaganda on the other. The reason I ask for the information is that I regard the inspection service as essential in any case, and I should like to know how much we are spending on that. The other activity seems to be very ill-advised under the circumstances, but until we know the extent of it, it seems a little difficult to criticize intelligently.
I should have to go through the data very carefully. It would require to be analysed in order to get the full list.
Could the Minister bring that information on a subsequent occasion?
I will try and get it for my hon. friend.
Perhaps the matter could stand over.
We will have to put this vote through to-night. I will get the information for my hon. friend on a later item if he will ask me about it.

In connection with another
item of the Immigration department?
Any other immigration item.

What action is the Department of Immigration taking in the case of the British Empire Steel Corporation who brings people in under contract and do not live up to that contract? Is the minister or the department taking any action to see that the contract is fulfilled?

I overlooked answering something on the same question at an earlier stage of the proceedings. I think my hon. friend from Bow- River (Mr. Garland) made a reference to three -very excellent chaps that I saw. Those men represented to us that they came to Canada on the strength of an advertisement inserted in the Glasgow Herald by the British Steel Corporation. The government of Canada has no control over the newspapers in Great Britain, but the government of Great Britain has control, and if that

Supply-Immigration
advertisement was inaccurate, they would have recourse through the government of that country.

I can quite understand
that we would have no control over any advertisement iput in the papers in the Old Country by the British Empire Steel Corporation, but when immigrants are brought into this country practically to work for such an organization as the British Steel Corporation or any other corporation, I should like to know what action the Department of Immigration would take, in case this corporation did not live up to the spirit of their contract.

My hon. friend is asking
rather a broad question, because if by implication the government should follow up all who publish alluring advertisements which are not quite right, and my hon. friend from Bow River is right, then the government of the province of Alberta is equally as culpable as any other body.

The minister has not
.caught the point of my question which is this: Here is an organization that practically to all intents and purposes makes contracts with men in the Old Country to come and work here. The question is this: What action does the Department of Immigration take with organizations or corporations which bring them into this country practically under contract and do not fulfil that contract?

The department are doing all they can. When men come to us with a contract, we do all we can to see that the parties live up to their contract. I will admit that if they do not live up to their contract this week, then, next week we might refuse admission to some person they attempted to bring in, but I do not see how we can go further. As to these three men, on their own statement, apart from not giving them work, the company had nc t been unkind to them, because they advanc d them money, and the men admitted in my office that the company had never pressed them for the return of that money, and they owed the company $580. I said to them, "Have you ever been pressed for this," and they said "No, because we did not have any work."	*

You cannot squeeze blood
out of a stone.
No.

I know of another case
where a man had been advanced money to
bring his family out here. But that is not the question I desired information about. We. may have corporations or individuals who bring people out by advertisements in other countries, but what action does
1 a.m. the Department of Immigration take, or can it take any action, to see that these contracts are lived up to?

No, but generally speaking
they are not lived up to?

There is no redress if
they are not lived up to?

Just the general law of the
country.
I do not think that is very much protection.
What is the routine adopted when a person in the Old Country wishes to come to Canada? To whom does he make application and what routine must he go through?

They may go to a booking
agent or an immigration agent, but in any event the booking agent has the immigration representative over there pass on him, and he gives him a permit. If our officer determines, that the subjects are not physically fit they are refused a permit to go on the ship.
Where is the physical examination made?
The final medical examination is made in Quebec or St. John, the port of landing. There is an advisory examination if it is considered necessary?
In the Old Country?
Yes.
Suppose the two examinations do not tally?

Our Canadian examination
decides it.
At Quebec?

Quebec, St. John or Halifax,
the port of landing.

Are the booking
agents government officials?

No, the booking agent might
be the railway agent or the steamship agent that sold the tickets.

Mr.. SPENCER: I should like to get from the minister the statement that our problem is more of a colonization problem than one of immigration.
Yes, now.

Particularly if we have
50,000	to 60,000 unemployed in Canada, and I for one refuse to believe that there is any more than a very small percentage of them unemployable. Many have gone off the farm. I have been approached by many of them who are very good farm hands, who have worked on farms for years-family men-but their work is quite uncertain for the entire year, and they have often approached me to see if there was any possible way they could be helped to farm by themselves. Here families are being brought over and started through direct or indirect government aid, they have been very anxious to know if something could not be done for them. These men are altogether better equipped for going farming than those who are being brought here; but on account of their family,-from three to eight of a family in some cases-the work that they have on a farm is very uncertain, and their usual action is to leave the country and go into the towns. I should like to ask the minister if something could not be done for that class of settler who would, if we could keep him, make a very excellent farmer, because they know how to farm, and they have been hired on farms for a good many years?

If my hon. friend means a
system of government advances, I say no.
Possibly a sympathetic system of rural credits might help.
Could the minister give the names of any societies or associations who may be carrying on with a view of earning grants to be made pursuant to order in council?

I have already put that on
record.
Why is it necessary to give these organizations money?

Both the Salvation Army and the Scottish Society have been doing good work. The Salvation Army gives after-care for four years to those whom it brings in, and if they are not satisfactory it takes them elsewhere without expense to the country.
Is it contemplated to grant moneys to any other society by order in council?	.
I have nothing in mind.
Why make it necessary to have orders in council for granting moneys to these societies? Why not have these amounts in the estimates so that it would be obvious to whom the money was given?
We are simply following the procedure that has been pursued for the last twenty-five or thirty years.
Has the minister put on Hansard already the various sums given to these organizations in the last fiscal year?
Last year we paid the Salvation Army $25,000, and we made a payment also to the Scottish Society.
Was anything paid to any other organization?
No.

Is the minister aware
that the government is really running two immigration departments, one a regular department under the Minister of Immigration, and the other an Immigration and Colonization department in connection with the Canadian National Railway Company, which is of course under the control of the government? Could there not be some co-ordination to eliminate duplication? The cost of immigration in connection with the Canadian National Railways is nearly $800,000 and the vote for immigration and colonization under the department of government at present under review amounts to something over $3,000,000. Is it not possible to harmonize the work by eliminating one of these departments? I am sure there must be some duplication. I have in mind the appointment of Dr. Black, who up to a year or so ago was the deputy minister of this department! He resigned and was immediately appointed to a position in the immigration department of the Canadian National Railways. His salary as Deputy Minister of Immigration was $6,000, but he was such a valuable man that Sir Henry Thornton gobbled him up at $15,000.
Ten thousand.
Well, $10,000. It would have been a simple matter for us to have asked him to continue to hang his hat and coat in this department instead of giving him $4,000 a year for moving.
And pay another man to replace him.

We have an excellent man in the person of Mr. Egan who is one of the most capable civil servants we have. I cannot

Supply-Immigration
understand why we should retain this other gentleman at $10,000 when we could have had his services at $6,000. And I do not know whether we want him at all. Do we want two departments of immigration, both striving for the same end? The Canadian National Railways are attempting by every possible means to bring people into the country, but there are in the department over which the minister (Mr. Robb) presides rules that prevent him from encroaching on the work of the other department. So there is a merry war between the two. I should like to see one of them eliminated so that we might know where we were going. Sir Henry Thornton in his annual report made the suggestion that in view of the great importance of immigration to the country the government might very well consider the question of naming a commission to deal with the whole immigration problem. He suggested that the commission should be on somewhat similar lines to the railway commission. I am not prepared to say whether this suggestion should be accepted or not. I suppose the object was that the immigration department of the Canadian National Railways and the Department of Immigration under the minister might bring their differences before the commission to have them settled. Whether that was in the mind of Sir Henry Thornton or not I do not know. But it does seem to me that that we might very well consider the question of appointing a standing committee of this House to deal with immigration problems. As I said on the budget, we have departments dealing with fish and fish culture, with mines, forests and all sorts of things, animate and inanimate.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Insects.

The Minister of Justice, forgetting that the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Motherwell) is immediately behind him, suggests insects. We are dealing with these too; we are dealing with bugs, onion maggots and other allied matters through select standing committees. But surely immigration is something that should occupy a sufficiently dignified position to demand from the government similar treatment. If we had had an immigration committee such as I suggest, we should have been deprived of the highly diverting evening we have had to-night, because all these matters could have been referred to that committee. Certainly, the minister would gain a great deal of useful information and assistance through such a committee, and now that his time is so much taken up in the Department of Finance, I am sure we are willing to lend him every
assistance possible. I suggest therefore that the government consider the question of appointing next year a select standing committee on Immigration and Colonization. I could say a great deal more on this question. Indeed, I feel somewhat like the poet-I would that my tongue could utter the thoughts that arise in me. The government is fully aware of my attitude on this question, and nothing that has been done since I have spoken on it has caused me to change my views, nor do I think that anything which the government may do in future will bring about such a change.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Would you have the member for Bow River on that committee?

The member for Bow River (Mr. Garland) would probably do fairly well if he were taken in hand by intelligent people and made to see that after all there is another point of view besides his own. I am free to confess that he impressed me towards the close of his remarks when he said that he had no objection whatever to allowing physically healthy people to come to the country. I must reckon that unto him for righteousness. I did not know that these were his views, and' I am willing to overlook many of the things he said in view of that conclusion. The hon. member for York-Sunbury (Mr. Hanson) also said that he would allow every white and healthy person to come to Canada; that would be part of his policy. Now, I find that his leader two or three days ago made a rather different statement in answer to a question put to him by the hon. member for Centre Winnipeg (Mr. Woods-wortth). At page 3806 I find the following:
Mr. Woodsworth: As long as we have anything like an open door immigration policy, how is the Canadian worker being protected?
Mr. Meighen: Well, I am not in favour of an open door immigration policy, any more than I am in favour of an open door trade policy.
We cannot, I fear, expect very much from the party immediately opposite me.
Sureiy my hon. friend is not in favour of an open door immigration policy? That would mean admitting everybody-good, bad or indifferent, healthy or ill.

My policy is known both to the House and to the country. The right hon. gentleman went on to explain himself. He said:
Certainly you cannot allow everybody into this country; nobody ever suggested it. The cheapest labour of the world we ought to bar entirely, and we do bar it. I would be the last to suggest that any other policy be adopted.

He was referring to yellow labour.	.

My recollection of my
leader's speech is that he was referring to oriental labour. Would my hon. friend (Mr. Jacobs) be in favour of an open door immigration from the Orient?

Absolutely not. I have
stated time and again that I am in favour of every healthy white person coming to this country. That is my policy. The leader of the opposition did not speak about oriental labour. Before he was interrupted by the hon. member for Centre Winnipeg he said:
It is possible to give preference and do so without invading the just rights of the Canadian worker. It must always be a case of Canada first, and until we are ready to stand up and proclaim Canada first, and act Canada first, then we may just as well resign ourselves to this sliding-back process which characterizes our drift to-day.
The leader of the opposition referred to the cheapest labour of the world. And where does that labour come from? It comes from China and Japan.

We have not that labour
now.
We have it at the coast.

Now, there seems to be no party at all which is ready to accept my policy, so I will start a party on my own account and look for recruits. And the first one whom I ^hall recruit into that party is the hon. member for Bow River-on the theory, of any port in a storm. I would start with him as a nucleus and we could secure other equally worthy supporters.

In answer to the question whether there are two immigration departments under the government, I would say yes and no. The Canadian Pacific Railway and the Canadian National Railways each have an immigration department, and the government of Canada must take care not to be allied with either. It would not be fair to do that.

Why not merge the two
departments under the government?

I am coming to that.
These three immigration departments are endeavouring to get closer together and work in greater harmony than they have done before, and there has been a good deal of cooperation with a view to reducing the expenditures under each of the departments and obviating any duplication.

Has the Canadian National
Railway Company an immigration office in London?

It has an immigration
ogganization in London which has control of European immigration so far as Canadian Nationjal propaganda is concerned. Each department, I can assure the committee, is doing its best to cut out overlapping and reduce expenses.

In view of the lateness of the hour, I would suggest that if this particular item were allowed to pass we might be given the assurance that we should be able to discuss the general policy of the department or some other item.
